Italian grammar & verb reference

Everything Italian explains with a rule

Twenty-two sections covering the parts of Italian that can actually be reasoned about — prepositions, tenses, pronouns, connectors — plus a conjugation library holding every form of 342 verbs. Written to be opened mid-sentence and closed thirty seconds later, not read from cover to cover.

What this is

A reference, not a course. It answers questions you already know you have.

It is good for

Settling a question mid-writing — a or in? che or cui? which past tense?
Understanding a rule you have been applying by instinct.
Drilling a specific weakness: one tense, one verb group, the irregulars only.
Checking any conjugation of any verb, in any of fourteen tenses.
Preparing for B2, where the subjunctive and the conditional decide your grade.

It is not

A beginner's course. It assumes you already know how nouns take gender, how adjectives agree, and roughly what a verb ending does — from about A2 upwards.

It has no exercises, no pronunciation, no feedback and no speaking practice. Those are the four things a reference cannot give you, and the four things that actually build a language.

If you are starting from zero, use a structured course for the first six months — a textbook, an app, or a teacher — and come here when the course introduces something and you want the whole rule rather than the lesson's slice of it. This reference will be far more useful in your second year than in your first.

Contents

Open a section directly, or search by what you are trying to say.

No section matches that.

How to get the most from it

Five habits that turn a reference into progress.

1 · Look up the rule, not the example

Every correction here comes with the rule that generates it. Remember the example and you have fixed one sentence. Remember the rule and you have fixed a category.

2 · Read sections 3 and 4 properly, once

Everything else can be dipped into. The two tense sections are the exception — they are the backbone, and most persistent errors trace back to them. Read them start to finish, then return as needed.

3 · Use the search inside long sections

Prepositions, false friends, the mistake log, the sentence bank and the verb library each have their own search. Type the English word and it will find the Italian.

4 · Drill with the verb library, not the whole list

Switch it to one tense, all verbs, then filter to irregular -ere verbs in the passato remoto. Narrow drilling beats broad review every time.

5 · Check your writing against section 12 before sending

The mistake log lists the twenty errors that survive longest, precisely because they are invisible while writing and obvious while reading. One pass catches most of them.

6 · Produce, do not just read

Cover the Italian column and generate it from the English. Recognition is not production, and only production is tested — in exams and in conversation alike.

Conventions

Green is correct, red is wrong

Italian in green is a form to use. Red marks a form to avoid, and is always paired with the correct version directly underneath.

Everything is translated

Every Italian example carries its English meaning. Nothing assumes you already know the sentence. Examples are drawn from ordinary professional situations, so they are usable as well as illustrative.

One file, nothing to install

This whole reference is a single HTML file, spreadsheet included. It opens on any device and works offline, with nothing to install.

How the conjugations were checked

Every form is generated from rules rather than typed, then compared form by form against an independent open-source conjugation engine — around thirteen thousand comparisons. Differences were reviewed by hand and the modern standard form kept.

Italian grammar reference · Section 1

Prepositions, and the articles they swallow

Italian has eight small words that decide whether a sentence sounds native or translated. Five of them fuse with the definite article, which is where most of the difficulty lives. Everything below is here to be looked up, not read once.

The eight Contractions Uses in detail A or IN Verb + preposition Time Common traps

The eight simple prepositions

Start here

Each one covers several jobs that English splits between different words. The list under each is what it actually does, not a translation.

di
of · from · than
  • possession
  • material
  • topic
  • origin (birthplace)
  • comparison
a
to · at · in
  • city or point
  • indirect object
  • clock time
  • manner
da
from · by · since
  • starting point
  • at someone's place
  • duration still running
  • purpose of an object
in
in · to · by
  • country or region
  • enclosed place
  • transport
  • time span
con
with
  • company
  • instrument
  • manner
su
on · about
  • surface
  • subject matter
  • approximation
per
for · through · to
  • recipient
  • purpose
  • finished duration
  • destination of travel
tra / fra
between · among · in
  • between two things
  • among a group
  • time from now

Preposition + article

Signature table

Five prepositions fuse with the definite article and become one word. This is not optional and it is not stylistic. Select any cell to see the contraction being built.

di + il → del il progetto del clientethe client's project
illol'laiglile

con may contract to col and coi, but modern writing prefers con il and con i. per, tra and fra never contract.

Which article does the noun take?

il masculine before most consonants · lo masculine before s+consonant, z, ps, gn, x, y · l' before any vowel · la feminine · i plural of il · gli plural of lo and l' · le feminine plural.

When there is no article, there is no contraction

Vado in ufficio. — I go to the office.
Vado nell'ufficio del direttore. — I go to the director's office.
The article appears once the noun is specified, and the preposition fuses with it.

What each preposition actually does

Every example is a sentence you could use at work. Search to jump to what you need.

DI — possession, material, topic, origin, comparison
Questo è il portfolio di Marco.This is Marco's portfolio.
Una scrivania di legno.A wooden desk.
Parliamo di budget domani.We'll talk about the budget tomorrow.
Sono di Napoli.I am from Naples. (born there)
Questa proposta è più chiara dell'altra.This proposal is clearer than the other one.
Lavoro di mattina.I work in the morning.
A — city, indirect object, clock time, manner
Domani vado a Milano.Tomorrow I'm going to Milan.
Ho mandato il file al cliente.I sent the file to the client.
La riunione comincia alle nove.The meeting starts at nine.
Preferisco disegnare a mano.I prefer to draw by hand.
Vengo a piedi.I'm coming on foot.
DA — origin, someone's place, ongoing duration, purpose
Vengo dall'aeroporto.I'm coming from the airport.
Stasera andiamo da Giulia.Tonight we're going to Giulia's place.
Lavoro in questo settore da dieci anni.I have been working in this field for ten years.
Ho molto da fare oggi.I have a lot to do today.
Mi servono gli occhiali da sole.I need sunglasses. (glasses for sun)
Il progetto è stato approvato dal direttore.The project was approved by the director.
IN — country, enclosed place, transport, time span
Mi trasferisco in Italia.I'm moving to Italy.
Sono in ufficio fino alle sei.I'm at the office until six.
Vado al lavoro in metropolitana.I go to work by underground.
Ho finito il lavoro in tre giorni.I finished the work in three days.
CON — company, instrument, manner
Lavoro con un piccolo team.I work with a small team.
Ho aperto il file con un altro programma.I opened the file with another program.
Rispondi con calma.Answer calmly.
SU — surface, subject matter, approximation
Le stampe sono sul tavolo.The prints are on the table.
Ho letto un articolo sul design italiano.I read an article about Italian design.
Il costo si aggira sui duemila euro.The cost is around two thousand euros.
PER — recipient, purpose, finished duration, destination
Questo messaggio è per te.This message is for you.
Studio l'italiano per lavorare in Europa.I study Italian in order to work in Europe.
Ho aspettato per due ore.I waited for two hours. (and stopped)
Parto per Roma lunedì.I'm leaving for Rome on Monday.
TRA / FRA — between, among, time from now
La differenza tra le due versioni è minima.The difference between the two versions is minimal.
Ti chiamo fra un'ora.I'll call you in an hour.
Tra colleghi ci si aiuta.Among colleagues, people help each other.
Nothing matches that. Try a shorter word.

A or IN with places

High-frequency

There is no logic to derive here. These are fixed and worth memorising as pairs.

A — cities, and these places

a Roma · a Milano · a Londra
a casa · a scuola · a teatro · a letto
al lavoro · al cinema · al bar · al ristorante · al mercato · al mare

IN — countries, regions, and these places

in Italia · in Toscana · in Spagna
in ufficio · in banca · in centro · in città
in montagna · in campagna · in palestra · in biblioteca · in cucina

The exception worth knowing

Plural and some masculine country names keep their article, so in contracts: negli Stati Uniti, nei Paesi Bassi, nel Regno Unito. Feminine singular countries do not: in Francia, in Germania.

Which preposition a verb demands

Before an infinitive, the verb decides the preposition. Getting this wrong is the single most audible error at B1.

Verb + A + infinitive

cominciare · iniziare · continuare · imparare · insegnare · riuscire · provare · aiutare · andare · venire · abituarsi

Sono riuscito a consegnare in tempo.
I managed to deliver on time.

Verb + DI + infinitive

finire · smettere · decidere · sperare · cercare · pensare · dimenticare · ricordarsi · promettere · evitare · rifiutare · fingere

Ho deciso di cambiare approccio.
I decided to change approach.

Verb + infinitive, no preposition

potere · volere · dovere · sapere · preferire · desiderare · fare · lasciare · vedere · sentire

Devo rivedere il file stasera.
I have to review the file tonight.

Verbs that take no preposition at all

English adds one before the noun and Italian does not: ascoltare · aspettare · cercare · guardare · pagare · chiedere

Aspetto l'autobus e ascolto un podcast.
I'm waiting for the bus and listening to a podcast.

Note: cercare appears in both lists. Before a noun it takes nothing (cerco lavoro); before an infinitive it takes di (cerco di capire).

Prepositions with time

Three of these carry a tense rule with them. Those are marked.

alle otto · all'una · a mezzogiornoat eight · at one · at midday
di mattina · di sera · di nottein the morning · in the evening · at night
a marzo · nel 2027in March · in 2027
in estate · d'invernoin summer · in winter
il lunedìon Mondays (every Monday)
lunedìon Monday (this coming one — no preposition)
da lunedì · dalle nove alle seifrom Monday · from nine to six
fra due orein two hours (from now)
in due orewithin two hours (time taken to finish)
per due orefor two hours — action finished, use a past tense
da due orefor two hours — action still running, use the PRESENT

Common traps

Read twice

These are the errors that survive longest, because English keeps suggesting them.

DA + present, not a past tense

If the action started in the past and is still going, Italian uses the present.

Ho lavorato qui da tre anni. Lavoro qui da tre anni. — I have been working here for three years.

A city, IN country

The size of the place decides the preposition, not the meaning of the sentence.

Vado in Roma. Vado a Roma e poi vado in Toscana.

No preposition after these verbs

English says "wait for", "listen to", "look at". Italian says none of them.

Aspetto per il treno. Aspetto il treno.

pensare A or pensare DI

A means to have someone or something in mind. Di introduces an opinion or an intention.

Penso a te. — I'm thinking of you. Penso di accettare. — I'm thinking of accepting. Cosa ne pensi? — What do you think about it?

essere DI or venire DA

Di gives your origin. Da gives the place you have just left.

Sono di Napoli. — I'm from Naples. (I was born there) Vengo da Napoli. — I'm coming from Naples. (just travelled)

partire PER, arrivare A

Leaving takes per; arriving takes a or in by the usual place rule.

Parto a Roma. Parto per Roma e arrivo a Roma alle sei.

TRA or FRA — decide by sound

They are identical in meaning. Pick the one that avoids repeating a sound in the next word.

fra tre giorni (not tra tre) tra fratelli (not fra fratelli)

The article is not optional

Once a noun takes an article, the preposition must fuse with it. Leaving them apart is a visible error.

Il nome di il cliente. Il nome del cliente.

Italian grammar reference · Section 2

Days, numbers, places, and what you do

These are usually filed under vocabulary, but each set carries a grammar rule with it — an article that appears or vanishes, a gender that decides a preposition, a vowel that drops. Learn the set and the rule together or you will learn the set twice.

DaysMonths & seasons NumbersOrder DatesCountries CitiesProfessions

The days of the week

Article changes meaning

All lowercase, always. All masculine except domenica. The first five carry a written accent on the final syllable, which is also where the stress falls.

lunedìMonday
martedìTuesday
mercoledìWednesday
giovedìThursday
venerdìFriday
sabatoSaturday
domenicaSunday

The article makes it a habit

Lunedì ho una riunione. — On Monday I have a meeting. (this coming Monday)
Il lunedì ho sempre una riunione. — On Mondays I always have a meeting. (every week)

Useful around them

il fine settimana — the weekend
nei giorni feriali · nei giorni festivi — on weekdays · on public holidays
dopodomani · l'altro ieri — the day after tomorrow · the day before yesterday

Months and seasons

Months are masculine and lowercase. Seasons split by gender, which changes the preposition.

gennaioJanuary
febbraioFebruary
marzoMarch
aprileApril
maggioMay
giugnoJune
luglioJuly
agostoAugust
settembreSeptember
ottobreOctober
novembreNovember
dicembreDecember

Saying "in a month"

a marzo — in March (most common)
nel mese di marzo — in the month of March (formal)
da marzo a giugno — from March to June

The four seasons

la primavera → in primavera — spring
l'estate (f) → in estate, d'estate — summer
l'autunno (m) → in autunno — autumn
l'inverno (m) → in inverno, d'inverno — winter

Numbers

Two spelling rules

Cardinal numbers are invariable — they do not agree with the noun. Only uno behaves like the indefinite article: un progetto, una riunione.

3tre

Tens, hundreds and above

21ventuno
22ventidue
23ventitré
28ventotto
30trenta

38trentotto
40quaranta

100.000centomila

The vowel drops before uno and otto

Tens ending in a vowel lose it when they meet uno or otto.

ventiuno · ventiotto · trentauno ventuno · ventotto · trentuno · trentotto · quarantotto

tre takes an accent in compounds

On its own it is bare; joined to a ten it is written with a final accent.

ventitre · trentatre ventitré · trentatré · quarantatré

cento and mille

cento never changes: duecento, novecento. mille becomes -mila in the plural: duemila, ventimila.

milione and miliardo are nouns

They take a plural and they take di before the thing counted.
due milioni di euro — two million euros

Punctuation runs the opposite way to English

Italian uses a full stop for thousands and a comma for decimals. 1.500,50 — one thousand five hundred and fifty cents, written 1,500.50 in English.

Order — first, second, third

These do agree

Unlike cardinals, ordinals are adjectives: they agree in gender and number with the noun. il primo giorno, la prima settimana, i primi risultati.

1ºprimofirst
2ºsecondosecond
3ºterzothird
4ºquartofourth
5ºquintofifth
6ºsestosixth
7ºsettimoseventh
8ºottavoeighth
9ºnononinth
10ºdecimotenth
11ºundicesimoeleventh
12ºdodicesimotwelfth
13ºtredicesimothirteenth
20ºventesimotwentieth
21ºventunesimotwenty-first
23ºventitreesimotwenty-third
26ºventiseiesimotwenty-sixth
100ºcentesimohundredth
1000ºmillesimothousandth

The first ten are irregular, the rest are built

From eleven onwards, drop the final vowel of the cardinal and add -esimo: undici → undicesimo, venti → ventesimo.

Numbers ending in tré and sei keep their vowel

The rule above stops here, because dropping the vowel would destroy the word.

ventitresimo · ventisesimo ventitreesimo · ventiseiesimo

Dates

One ordinal, then cardinals for the rest of the month. This trips up almost everyone once.

WRITING A DATE
il primo maggiothe first of May — the only day that uses an ordinal
il due maggio · il quindici marzothe second of May · the fifteenth of March
Oggi è il ventitré aprile.Today is the twenty-third of April.
Quanti ne abbiamo oggi? — Ne abbiamo dodici.What's the date today? — It's the twelfth.
YEARS AND DECADES
nel 2027 — nel duemilaventisettein 2027
negli anni Novantain the nineties
dal 2020 al 2024from 2020 to 2024

Countries and nationalities

Gender decides the preposition

Countries have gender and take an article when you talk about them. The article usually disappears after in — except for the plural ones, which is the whole difficulty.

feminine masculine plural

l'ItaliaItaly
la FranciaFrance
la SpagnaSpain
la GermaniaGermany
l'InghilterraEngland
la GreciaGreece
la SvizzeraSwitzerland
la CinaChina
l'IndiaIndia
il PortogalloPortugal
il BelgioBelgium
il GiapponeJapan
il BrasileBrazil
il CanadaCanada
il MessicoMexico
il MaroccoMorocco
il PerùPeru
gli Stati Unitithe United States
i Paesi Bassithe Netherlands
il Regno Unitothe United Kingdom
gli Emirati Arabi Unitithe UAE

Going there: no article

Vado in Italia · in Portogallo · in Giappone · in Argentina

Unless the name is plural or a phrase

Then the article stays and in contracts with it.

negli Stati Uniti · nei Paesi Bassi · nel Regno Unito nell'Italia del Nord — the article also returns when the country is modified

Nationalities and languages are lowercase

Sono italiano. · È francese. · Sono egiziana.
Languages are masculine: l'italiano, l'inglese. After parlare the article is normally dropped: Parlo italiano, but Studio l'italiano.

Cities

Simpler than countries, with one exception worth memorising.

THE PATTERN
Vado a Roma. · Abito a Milano.I'm going to Rome. · I live in Milan.
Sono di Firenze.I'm from Florence. (born there)
Vengo da Torino.I'm coming from Turin. (just travelled)
Roma è bella. · Milano è cara.Rome is beautiful. · Milan is expensive.
CITIES WHOSE NAME CONTAINS AN ARTICLE
il Cairo → al CairoCairo → to / in Cairo
L'Aquila → all'AquilaL'Aquila → to / in L'Aquila
La Spezia → alla SpeziaLa Spezia → to / in La Spezia

City names are treated as feminine

Whatever the ending, an adjective describing a city takes the feminine form: Milano è industriale, Napoli è antica.

Professions

The article rule

Which verb you use decides whether the profession takes an article. This is a small rule with a very audible effect.

essere — no article

Sono ingegnere. — I'm an engineer.
È insegnante. — She's a teacher.

fare — article required

Faccio l'ingegnere. — I work as an engineer.
Fa l'insegnante. — She works as a teacher.

Add an adjective and the article returns

Sono un bravo ingegnere. — I'm a good engineer.

The most common version of this error

English always wants an article here. Italian does not, after essere.

Sono un ingegnere. Sono ingegnere.

How the feminine is formed

-O BECOMES -A
impiegato → impiegataoffice worker
fotografo → fotografaphotographer
cuoco → cuocacook
veterinario → veterinariavet
-TORE BECOMES -TRICE
direttore → direttricedirector
illustratore → illustratriceillustrator
traduttore → traduttricetranslator
scrittore → scrittricewriter
-E AND -ISTA STAY THE SAME — ONLY THE ARTICLE CHANGES
il / la insegnanteteacher
il / la giornalistajournalist
il / la dentistadentist
l'artista (m and f)artist — plural: gli artisti, le artiste
-ESSA IS ADDED
studente → studentessastudent
professore → professoressaprofessor
dottore → dottoressadoctor, and any graduate
BORROWED WORDS DO NOT CHANGE AT ALL
il / la designer · il / la managerdesigner · manager
il / la freelance · il / la partnerfreelancer · partner

First, the mood

Indicativo

States things as fact. Eight tenses.

Congiuntivo

Marks a clause as opinion, doubt or desire. Four tenses.

Condizionale

Politeness, wishes, and the result of a hypothesis. Two tenses.

Imperativo

Commands and instructions. One set of forms.

How to study this section

  1. Start with the building blocksPersons, stems, endings, auxiliaries and participles. Everything else is built from them.
  2. Learn the tenses in this orderPresente → passato prossimo → imperfetto → futuro → condizionale → congiuntivo presente → trapassato prossimo → congiuntivo imperfetto → the rest.
  3. Use the test at the bottom of each pageIt marks itself, shows the rule behind every miss, and logs your mistakes for later practice.
Foundations

Building blocks

Every Italian verb form is a stem plus an ending, sometimes behind an auxiliary. Learn these seven pieces and each tense page becomes a matter of applying them.

Stem + endingPersonsParticiplesAuxiliariesEssere or avereReflexivesGerund

Stem + ending

An Italian infinitive ends in -are, -ere or -ire. Remove that ending and you have the stem. Every conjugated form is the stem plus an ending that tells you who, when and how.

parlare
credere
dormire

Three conjugations, then one sub-group: about half of the -ire verbs are -isc- verbs and insert -isc- in the present and the present subjunctive (finisco, capisco). The verb library marks which is which.

The six persons

personpronounmeaningnotes
1st singularioI
2nd singulartuyou (informal)friends, family, peers
3rd singularlui / leihe / shealso Lei (formal “you”) with the same verb form
1st pluralnoiwe
2nd pluralvoiyou (plural)
3rd plurallorotheyalso Loro (very formal plural “you”)

The pronoun is normally dropped, because the ending already tells you who is acting: parlo is “I speak”. Add the pronoun only to contrast, to stress, or when the form is ambiguous (the congiuntivo io / tu / lui all look the same).

Past participles

Used in every compound tense. Regular: -are → -ato (parlato), -ere → -uto (venduto), -ire → -ito (dormito, finito). Of the 342 verbs in the library, 105 have an irregular participle, grouped below by shape.

Participles in -so (39)

Essere or avere?

Essere

• verbs of motion and arrival (andare, venire, arrivare, partire, entrare, uscire, tornare)
• change of state (nascere, morire, diventare, crescere)
• staying (essere, stare, rimanere, restare)
• all reflexive verbs (mi sono lavato)
• most impersonal verbs (piacere, sembrare, bastare, succedere)

Avere

• every verb with a direct object (ho mangiato una mela)
• most intransitive verbs of activity (ho lavorato, ho dormito, ho riso)
• avere and (in practice) most other verbs
• modal verbs: they borrow the auxiliary of the following verb (sono voluto andare, ho voluto mangiare)

The 37 non-reflexive verbs in the library that take essere:

accadereandareapparireappartenerearrivarebastarecaderecostarecresceredipenderedispiacerediventaredurareentrareesistereesserefuggiremorirenascereoccorrereparerepartirepiacererestarerimanereritornareriuscirescapparescompariresembraresparirestaresuccederetornareuscirevalerevenire

Some verbs take either, depending on whether they have a direct object: La vita è cambiata / Ho cambiato idea; Il film è finito / Ho finito il film; Sono salito al terzo piano / Ho salito le scale.

Reflexive verbs

The action returns to the subject. The pronoun comes before the conjugated verb and changes with the person: mi · ti · si · ci · vi · si. Always essere in compound tenses.

Mi alzo alle sette.I get up at seven.
Ci siamo conosciuti a Roma.We met in Rome.
Si è laureata l'anno scorso.She graduated last year.

The gerund

Stem + -ando (-are) or -endo (-ere, -ire): parlando, vendendo, dormendo. Irregular ones: facendo, dicendo, bevendo, ponendo, traducendo. It describes how, why or when, and it forms the progressive with stare.

Sto studiando.I'm studying (right now).
Parlando con lui, ho capito tutto.Talking to him, I understood everything.
Studiando ogni giorno, migliorerai.By studying every day, you'll improve.

Indicativo

Presente

PresentA1
stem + o · i · a · iamo · ate / ete / ite · ano / ono

What is true now, what happens regularly, and what is about to happen. The most-used tense in spoken Italian, including for the future.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The Italian present covers three English forms at once: I work, I am working and I do work are all lavoro. You are never obliged to use a separate progressive (sto lavorando exists, but only when you want to stress “right now, this minute”).

It also runs forward into the near future, where English needs a future form. Domani parto is more natural than domani partirò. And it does one job that English gives to the perfect: with da, it describes something that started in the past and is still going on. With an affirmative sentence a past tense is wrong there (Studio italiano da due anni, not Ho studiato italiano da due anni). In a negative sentence the passato prossimo is fine: Non lo vedo da due anni and Non l’ho visto da due anni are both used.

The only real work is learning the three conjugations and their irregular verbs. Most of the very common verbs (essere, avere, andare, fare, dire, venire, potere, volere, dovere) are irregular in the present, so they are the first ones to memorise.

How to build it

  1. Take the infinitive and remove -are / -ere / -ireparlare → parl- · credere → cred- · dormire → dorm-
  2. Add the six endings for the groupThe -are group uses a in the lui form (parla); -ere and -ire use e (crede, dorme). The loro form is -ano for -are but -ono for -ere and -ire.
  3. For about half of the -ire verbs add -isc-In io, tu, lui and loro, these verbs insert -isc- (finisco). Noi and voi do not. There is no rule that tells you which verbs do this; the verb library marks each one.

Irregulars

About one verb in eight is irregular in the present, and they are the most common ones. The highlighted part is where the verb departs from the regular pattern. Notice the shape: the io and loro forms usually share a stem (vado … vanno, vengo … vengono), while noi and voi stay regular (andiamo, andate).

Uses

A fact or a habit

What is true in general, or what you do regularly.

Lavoro in una banca.I work in a bank.
Il sabato studio sempre in biblioteca.On Saturdays I always study in the library.
L'acqua bolle a cento gradi.Water boils at one hundred degrees.

Right now

Italian does not need the progressive. Use stare + gerundio only to stress that it is happening this very moment.

Leggo un libro.I'm reading a book.
Sto leggendo, non disturbarmi!I'm reading right now, don't disturb me!

The near future

When the plan is fixed or certain, the present is the natural choice.

Domani parto per Milano.Tomorrow I'm leaving for Milan.
Stasera cuciniamo a casa.Tonight we're cooking at home.

Something that started in the past and is still going on

Present + da + a period of time or a starting point.

Studio l'italiano da un anno.I have been studying Italian for a year.
Abito qui da gennaio.I've lived here since January.

Traps

The DA trap

If the action is still running, the verb stays in the present, however long it has been going on.

Ho studiato l'italiano da due anni.Studio l'italiano da due anni.

-isc- verbs

Capire, finire, preferire, spedire and many others need -isc- in four persons.

Io capo. · Loro preferono.Io capisco. · Loro preferiscono.

Spelling of -care, -gare, -ciare, -giare

Hard sounds stay hard: an h appears before i or e. In -ciare / -giare the i of the stem disappears before another i.

Tu cerci. · Tu mangii.Tu cerchi. · Tu mangi.

Compare

vs Imperfetto

The present describes the situation now; the imperfetto describes the same kind of situation in the past (lavoro → lavoravo).

Passato prossimo

Present perfect · compound pastA2
avere or essere in the present + past participle

The everyday past tense: things that happened and are over. It covers both “I have finished” and “I finished”.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

This is the past tense you will use most. Despite the English label, it covers both I have finished and I finished, because Italian does not force the distinction English makes. It reports events: things that happened, started and ended.

Two decisions come with it. First, the auxiliary: most verbs take avere, but verbs of motion and change of state take essere, and so do all reflexive verbs. Second, with essere the participle agrees with the subject in gender and number, so a woman writes sono andata. With avere it does not agree, unless a direct object pronoun (lo, la, li, le) comes first.

A few verbs change auxiliary depending on whether they have a direct object: La mia vita è cambiata (nothing is acted upon, essere) but Ho cambiato idea (there is an object, avere).

How to build it

  1. Choose the auxiliaryavere for most verbs; essere for motion and change (andare, venire, arrivare, partire, nascere, diventare), for “to be” verbs (essere, stare, rimanere) and for every reflexive verb.
  2. Conjugate the auxiliary in the presentho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno · sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono
  3. Add the past participle-are → -ato (parlato) · -ere → -uto (venduto) · -ire → -ito (dormito). Many -ere verbs have irregular participles (see the table below).
  4. With essere, make the participle agreeLui è andato · lei è andata · loro sono andati · loro (f.) sono andate.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioho mangiatosono andato / andata

lui / leiha mangiatoè andato / andata
noiabbiamo mangiatosiamo andati / andate
voiavete mangiatosiete andati / andate
lorohanno mangiatosono andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)

Irregular participles

The verbs you will need most. The full list of 105 is in the building blocks.

fatto faredetto direvisto vederepreso prenderemesso metterescritto scrivereletto leggerechiesto chiedererisposto rispondereaperto aprirechiuso chiuderedeciso decidereperso perderevissuto viverevenuto venirestato esserebevuto bererotto romperescelto sceglierecorso correrenato nascererimasto rimanerespeso spendereofferto offrirescoperto scoprire

Uses

A finished event

Something that happened, whether a minute ago or ten years ago.

Ho consegnato il progetto ieri.I delivered the project yesterday.
Siamo andati insieme.We went together.
Nel 2010 mi sono laureato.I graduated in 2010.

A recent action with results now

Where English uses the present perfect.

Ho finito proprio adesso.I've just finished.
Hai già mangiato?Have you eaten yet?
Non ho ancora risposto.I haven't replied yet.

A sequence of events

Each action is a new step in the story.

Mi sono alzato, ho fatto colazione e sono uscito.I got up, had breakfast and went out.

A completed period

When the whole period is over, even if long.

Ho lavorato lì per dieci anni.I worked there for ten years.
Ieri ho studiato tutto il giorno.Yesterday I studied all day.

Traps

The auxiliary is not optional

Choosing avere for an essere verb is one of the most audible errors in spoken Italian.

Ho andato al lavoro. · Ho stato a Roma.Sono andato al lavoro. · Sono stato a Roma.

Reflexives always take essere

Even when English says “have”.

Mi ho lavato.Mi sono lavato.

The pronoun forces agreement

With a direct object pronoun before the verb, the participle agrees with it even with avere.

Le stampe? Le ho visto.Le stampe? Le ho viste.

Change of auxiliary

Cambiare, finire, cominciare, passare, salire, scendere: essere when the subject is what changes, avere when there is a direct object.

La mia vita ha cambiato quel giorno.La mia vita è cambiata quel giorno. · Quel giorno ho cambiato idea.

Compare

vs Imperfetto

Passato prossimo reports the event; imperfetto sets the scene. Pioveva (scene) quando sono uscito (event).

vs Passato remoto

In central and northern speech the passato prossimo has replaced the passato remoto for everything; use it.

Imperfetto

ImperfectA2
stem + avo / evo / ivo · only a handful of irregular verbs

A different way of looking at the past: not the event, but the situation around it. Habits, descriptions, background and what was in progress.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The imperfetto is not simply another past tense; it is a different way of looking at the past. Where the passato prossimo reports an event with a beginning and an end, the imperfetto describes a situation with neither. Use it for habits (what you used to do), for description (how things and people were), for age, weather, time and feelings, and for an action that was in progress when something else happened.

A useful test: if you could say used to, was doing or would (always) in English, you almost certainly need the imperfetto. Another: if the sentence answers “what was it like?”, it is imperfetto; if it answers “what happened?”, it is passato prossimo.

The good news is that it is the most regular tense in the language. Only essere, fare, dire, bere and the verbs derived from Latin short forms (porre, trarre, condurre and their families) are irregular, and even those just keep an older, longer stem.

How to build it

  1. Take the infinitive and remove -reparlare → parla- · credere → crede- · dormire → dormi-
  2. Add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vanoThe vowel before -v- comes from the infinitive, so you get -avo, -evo, -ivo. Every verb, including -isc- verbs, follows this (finivo, not finiscevo).
  3. Check the irregular onesessere → ero · fare → facevo · dire → dicevo · bere → bevevo · porre → ponevo · tradurre → traducevo · trarre → traevo.

Endings

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

Only a handful of verbs are irregular here, and in every one the stem simply keeps the older, longer form: fa(c)-evo, di(c)-evo, be(v)-evo. The verbs in -rre (porre, trarre, condurre…) do the same.

Uses

A habit in the past

“Used to” or “would always”.

Da studente disegnavo ogni giorno.As a student I used to draw every day.
Ogni estate andavamo al mare.Every summer we would go to the sea.

Description: people, places, things

How things were.

La casa era piccola ma luminosa.The house was small but bright.
Mia nonna aveva i capelli bianchi.My grandmother had white hair.

Age, time, weather, feelings

The conditions around an event.

Avevo vent'anni.I was twenty.
Erano le otto e pioveva.It was eight o'clock and it was raining.
Ero stanco e avevo fame.I was tired and hungry.

An action in progress when something happened

Imperfetto is the frame; passato prossimo is the interruption.

Mentre lavoravo, è arrivato il cliente.While I was working, the client arrived.
Uscivo di casa quando ha squillato il telefono.I was leaving the house when the phone rang.

Two things at the same time

Both verbs in the imperfetto.

Lui cucinava e io apparecchiavo.He was cooking and I was laying the table.

Politeness, thoughts and reported feelings

Softening a request, or saying what you were thinking.

Volevo un caffè, per favore.I wanted a coffee, please. (softer than “voglio”)
Pensavo che fosse più facile.I thought it was easier.

Traps

Not for completed events

A finished, bounded action takes the passato prossimo, however far back it was.

Ieri lavoravo fino alle otto e finivo il progetto.Ieri ho lavorato fino alle otto e ho finito il progetto.

A period with clear limits

When a period has a clear beginning and end (for ten years, all day), the passato prossimo is the normal choice. The imperfetto stays correct for a repeated habit inside the period: Ogni giorno lavoravo per otto ore.

Abitavo a Torino per dieci anni.Ho abitato a Torino per dieci anni.

-isc- does not appear

The imperfetto is built from the infinitive, not the present.

Io finiscevo.Io finivo.

Compare

vs Passato prossimo

Some verbs change meaning between the two. Sapevo = I knew · ho saputo = I found out. Conoscevo = I knew (someone) · ho conosciuto = I met. Volevo = I wanted · ho voluto = I insisted/chose to. Potevo = I could (was able in principle) · ho potuto = I managed to.

Futuro semplice

Simple futureA2
infinitive minus -e (with -are → -er-) + ò · ai · à · emo · ete · anno

Future plans and predictions, but also something native speakers use all the time: a guess about the present.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

Italians use the present for near or certain future events far more than English speakers do, so domani parto is more natural than domani partirò. The future tense is for things that are further off, less sure, or part of a promise or a prediction.

What the futuro does distinctively is express probability about the present: a guess or an inference. Sarà stanco can mean “he will be tired”, but very often it means “he must be tired”. This use is extremely common in speech and almost never taught early.

The other point English speakers miss: after quando, appena and dopo che referring to the future, Italian usually uses a future in both clauses (the present is also common when the future meaning is clear), where English uses a present in one: Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò (When I arrive, I'll call you).

How to build it

  1. Take the infinitive and drop the final -eparlare → parlar- · vendere → vender- · dormire → dormir-
  2. For -are verbs change a to eparlar- → parler-: parlerò. (This is the same stem as the condizionale.)
  3. Add the endings, which are the same for every verb-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno (these come from the present of avere).
  4. Keep the sound hard or soft-care / -gare → cher- / gher-: cercherò, pagherò · -ciare / -giare drop the i: comincerò, mangerò.

Endings

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

-areparlare-erecredere-iredormire
ioparleròcrederòdormirò
tuparleraicrederaidormirai
lui / leiparleràcrederàdormirà
noiparleremocrederemodormiremo
voiparleretecrederetedormirete
loroparlerannocrederannodormiranno

Compare the -are stem: parlerò, not parlarò.

Uses

Plans and predictions further off

Something not immediate.

L'anno prossimo mi trasferirò.Next year I'll move.
Domani pioverà in tutto il Nord.Tomorrow it will rain across the north.

Promises and decisions made on the spot

Often with a firm tone.

Ti chiamerò appena possibile.I'll call you as soon as I can.
Lo farò io.I'll do it.

A guess about the present

An inference about what is probably true now.

Sarà in riunione.He must be in a meeting.
Quanti anni avrà? Avrà trent'anni.How old do you reckon he is? About thirty.

Future in both clauses

After quando, appena, dopo che about the future.

Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò.When I arrive, I'll call you.
Appena saprò qualcosa, ti scriverò.As soon as I know something, I'll write to you.

Traps

Present stem in the future

The stem comes from the infinitive, not the present.

Io pagerò. · Io mangierò.Io pagherò. · Io mangerò.

Mixing the future with the present stem of -are

The a of -are becomes e in the future, so parlare gives parlerò, not parlarò.

Io parlarò. · Io mangiarò.Io parlerò. · Io mangerò.

Compare

vs Presente

For the near, certain future the present is the natural choice. Use the futuro for distance, doubt and promises.

vs Futuro anteriore

Future: what will happen. Futuro anteriore: what will already have happened by then.

Condizionale

Condizionale presente

Present conditionalA2
future stem + ei · esti · ebbe · emmo · este · ebbero

Politeness, wishes, advice and the result of a hypothesis. The tense that makes you sound civilised.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

It shares its stem with the future, so every irregular future stem you know gives you the conditional free. Its main work in daily life is politeness: vorrei rather than voglio is the difference between asking and demanding. It also gives advice (dovresti), expresses wishes (mi piacerebbe), and forms the result half of a hypothesis (se avessi tempo, verrei).

Italian journalism uses it for a fourth purpose: reporting something that has not been verified (il ministro sarebbe già partito, “the minister has reportedly already left”).

How to build it

  1. Take the future stemparler-, creder-, dormir-, andr-, vorr-
  2. Add the endings-ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero
  3. Mind the hard and soft soundscercherei, pagherei, mangerei, comincerei

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

The stems are the same as in the futuro semplice: only the endings change.

Uses

Politeness

Requests and offers.

Potrebbe aiutarmi?Could you help me?

Advice

Dovere and potere in the conditional.

Dovresti riposare un po'.You should rest a bit.
Potresti chiedere a lui.You could ask him.

Wishes and tastes

What you would like.

Mi piacerebbe vivere in Italia.I'd love to live in Italy.

The result half of a hypothesis

Paired with the congiuntivo imperfetto.

Se avessi più tempo, studierei di più.If I had more time, I'd study more.
Al posto tuo, accetterei.In your position, I'd accept.

Unverified news

Reported speech in journalism.

Secondo il giornale, sarebbe già partito.According to the paper, he has reportedly already left.

Traps

Voglio is blunt

In a shop, a restaurant or an email, the present sounds like a demand.

Voglio un caffè.Vorrei un caffè. · Un caffè, per favore.

Future stem, not present stem

The stem is the same as the future.

Io andarei. · Io venirei.Io andrei. · Io verrei.

Compare

vs Futuro semplice

Same stem, different endings: parlerò (will) vs parlerei (would).

vs Condizionale passato

Presente: would (now / later). Passato: would have (but did not).

Imperativo

Imperativo

ImperativeA2
tu: stem + a / i · Lei: congiuntivo · noi, voi: as the present

Orders, instructions, invitations and advice. The negative tu is special, and pronouns attach to the end of most forms.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The tu form of -are verbs looks like the lui form (parla), while -ere and -ire verbs use the tu form of the present (credi, dormi). The formal Lei imperative simply borrows the congiuntivo present (parli, creda, dorma). The noi and voi imperatives are the same as the present indicative (parliamo, parlate), and loro (formal plural) borrows the congiuntivo (parlino).

Two details cause most errors. The negative tu is non + the plain infinitive (non parlare), not the imperative. And pronouns attach to the end of the tu, noi and voi forms (dimmi, andiamoci, ditemelo) but sit in front of the Lei form (mi dica).

Several very common verbs have short imperatives: va' / vai, fa' / fai, di', da' / dai, sta' / stai. With pronouns attached, these double the first consonant of the pronoun: dimmi, fallo, dammi, stammi (but not with gli: digli).

How to build it

  1. tu-are: -a (parla!) · -ere: -i (credi!) · -ire: -i (dormi!, finisci!)
  2. Lei and loro: congiuntivo presenteparli · creda · dorma · finisca · (loro) parlino
  3. noi and voi: same as the presentparliamo · parlate · crediamo · credete · dormiamo · dormite
  4. Negative tu: non + infinitivenon parlare · non credere · non dormire

Endings

-areparlare-erecredere-iredormire-ire (-isc-)finire
tuparlacredidormifinisci
Leiparlicredadormafinisca
noiparliamocrediamodormiamofiniamo
voiparlatecredetedormitefinite
Loroparlinocredanodormanofiniscano
negative tunon parlarenon crederenon dormirenon finire

The Lei and Loro forms are the congiuntivo presente. The noi and voi forms are the same as the present indicative. Only tu has its own forms, plus the negative tu with the infinitive.

Uses

Orders and instructions

Recipes, directions, workplace instructions.

Apri la porta, per favore.Open the door, please.
Prenda la seconda a destra.Take the second right. (formal)

Invitations and advice

Friendly and polite.

Dimmi tutto.Tell me everything.
Mi dica pure.Do tell me. (formal)
Andiamoci insieme.Let's go there together.

Negatives

Tu uses non + infinitive; all others use the usual form.

Non preoccuparti.Don't worry.
Non vada via!Don't leave! (formal)
Non fate rumore.Don't make noise. (plural)

Addressing a group

Voi form.

Scusate il ritardo.Sorry for the delay.
Entrate pure.Come in.

Traps

The negative tu is not the imperative

For tu only, negation replaces the imperative with the infinitive.

Non parla! · Non dimmi!Non parlare! · Non dirmi!

Pronoun position

Attached for tu, noi, voi; in front for Lei.

Dicami! · Mi di'!Mi dica! · Dimmi!

-isc- verbs keep it in the tu form

The tu imperative of an -isc- verb is like the present: finisci!, capisci! Noi and voi do not take -isc-: finiamo, finite.

Fini il lavoro!Finisci il lavoro!

vs Congiuntivo presente

Lei and loro imperatives are the congiuntivo presente.

Indicativo

Trapassato prossimo

Past perfectB1
avere or essere in the imperfetto + past participle

The past before the past: it marks something that had already happened before the moment you are describing.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

Whenever you tell a story out of sequence, mentioning something that had already happened before the moment you are describing, this is the tense that marks it. English does the same with had, so the concept is familiar; what is unfamiliar is that Italian expects it far more consistently and sounds careless without it.

It is built exactly like the passato prossimo, but with the auxiliary in the imperfetto: ho mangiato → avevo mangiato, sono andato → ero andato. The choice of auxiliary and the agreement rules are identical.

It is often triggered by words such as già, non… ancora, appena, prima, dopo che, or by a clause that gives a reason for something in the past.

How to build it

  1. Choose the auxiliary exactly as for the passato prossimoavere or essere; reflexives take essere.
  2. Put it in the imperfettoavevo, avevi, aveva, avevamo, avevate, avevano · ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano
  3. Add the past participleAgree with the subject when the auxiliary is essere: lei era partita, loro erano partiti.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioavevo mangiatoero andato / andata
tuavevi mangiatoeri andato / andata
lui / leiaveva mangiatoera andato / andata
noiavevamo mangiatoeravamo andati / andate
voiavevate mangiatoeravate andati / andate
loroavevano mangiatoerano andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioavevoero
tuavevieri
lui / leiavevaera
noiavevamoeravamo
voiavevateeravate
loroavevanoerano

Uses

An action completed before another past moment

The reference point is itself in the past.

Quando sono arrivato, avevi già mangiato.When I arrived, you had already eaten.
Non sapevo che fosse partito: era partito la settimana prima.I didn't know he had left; he had left the week before.

The reason or background for a past event

Explaining why something was the way it was.

Ero stanco perché avevo lavorato tutta la notte.I was tired because I had worked all night.
Non l'ho riconosciuto: era cambiato molto.I didn't recognise him; he had changed a lot.

Reported speech

After a past reporting verb, what was already done.

Mi ha detto che aveva già pagato.He told me he had already paid.

Traps

Passato prossimo for the earlier event

When both actions are past and one came first, the earlier one wants the trapassato.

Quando sono arrivato, hai già mangiato.Quando sono arrivato, avevi già mangiato.

Wrong auxiliary

Same as passato prossimo.

Avevo andato.Ero andato.

Compare

vs Passato prossimo

Passato prossimo: the main events in order. Trapassato: what had happened before them.

Futuro anteriore

Future perfectB1
avere or essere in the futuro + past participle

An action finished before another point in the future; and a guess about something in the past.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

It marks an action that will be completed before another future action or time. It also carries the same probability sense as the simple future, but pointed at the past: avrà avuto trent'anni means “he must have been about thirty”.

In sentences with quando, appena, dopo che, Italian often uses the futuro anteriore where English uses a present perfect: Quando avrò finito, ti chiamerò (When I've finished, I'll call you).

How to build it

  1. Take the futuro of the auxiliaryavrò, avrai, avrà, avremo, avrete, avranno · sarò, sarai, sarà, saremo, sarete, saranno
  2. Add the past participleAgree when using essere.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioavrò mangiatosarò andato / andata
tuavrai mangiatosarai andato / andata
lui / leiavrà mangiatosarà andato / andata
noiavremo mangiatosaremo andati / andate
voiavrete mangiatosarete andati / andate
loroavranno mangiatosaranno andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioavròsarò
tuavraisarai
lui / leiavràsarà
noiavremosaremo
voiavretesarete
loroavrannosaranno

Uses

Finished before a future moment

Often with entro, fra, quando, appena.

Quando avrò finito, ti chiamo.When I've finished, I'll call you.
Fra un anno mi sarò trasferito.In a year I will have moved.

A guess about the past

Probability.

Avrà dimenticato l'appuntamento.He must have forgotten the appointment.
Non è ancora arrivato: avrà trovato traffico.He hasn't arrived yet; he must have hit traffic.

Traps

Present perfect word for word

After quando / appena about the future, use futuro anteriore, not passato prossimo.

Appena ho finito, ti chiamerò.Appena avrò finito, ti chiamerò.

Compare

vs Futuro semplice

Futuro semplice: will happen. Futuro anteriore: will already have happened.

Congiuntivo

Congiuntivo presente

Present subjunctiveB1
stem + i · i · i · iamo · iate · ino (-are) · a · a · a · iamo · iate · ano (-ere / -ire)

Opinion, doubt, wish and emotion in a subordinate clause: not stating a fact but presenting a view.

ExplanationTriggersHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The congiuntivo is not a tense but a mood: a grammatical signal that what follows is presented as a view, a wish, a doubt or an emotion rather than as a plain statement of fact. A few triggers take it even for facts you accept as true (Mi dispiace che sia successo, benché sia piovuto), so learn the triggers as a list. It appears in a subordinate clause after opinion, doubt, emotion, hope, will and fear, and after a fixed set of conjunctions. English lost almost all of this, which is why it feels arbitrary. It is not, but it does have to be learned as a list of triggers.

Two practical details. First: io, tu and lui share the same form, so add the pronoun whenever the subject would otherwise be unclear (spero che tu stia bene). Second: when the main clause and the subordinate clause have the same subject, prefer di + infinitive (Penso di avere ragione). Penso che io abbia ragione is possible when you want to stress the subject, but it is the marked choice.

The present subjunctive refers to the same time as the main verb or to the future. For something already done, use the congiuntivo passato.

What triggers it

Use it in the subordinate clause after these.

Opinionpenso / credo / ritengo / mi sembra che · pare che
Doubtdubito / non sono sicuro / non so se · è possibile che
Wish, will, requestvoglio / desidero / spero / preferisco che · ti chiedo che
Emotionsono contento / mi dispiace / ho paura / mi stupisce che
Impersonal expressionsè necessario / bisogna / è meglio / è un peccato che
Conjunctionsbenché · sebbene · nonostante · affinché · purché · a meno che · prima che · senza che · qualunque · comunque (meaning “however”: comunque vada; the connective Comunque, vengo domani needs no subjunctive)

How to build it

  1. Take the stem of the io form of the presentparl-, cred-, dorm-, fin-
  2. Use the right pattern for the group-are: -i in the first three persons; all others: -a. Noi is always -iamo and voi -iate (the same as the indicative noi, except for voi).
  3. -isc- verbs keep -isc-finisca, finisca, finisca, finiamo, finiate, finiscano.

Endings

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

Irregulars

Most irregular present subjunctives are built on the io form of the present: vado → vada, vengo → venga, dico → dica. The exceptions (essere, avere, sapere, dare, stare, volere) are the ones to memorise. Notice that noi and voi are usually regular.

Uses

Opinion and belief

After verbs of thinking when you are not certain.

Penso che sia la scelta giusta.I think it's the right choice.
Credo che lui abbia ragione.I believe he's right.

Wish and will

Hoping, wanting, preferring something to happen.

Voglio che tu venga.I want you to come.
Spero che tu stia bene.I hope you're well.

Emotion

Feelings about a fact.

Mi dispiace che tu sia stanco.I'm sorry you're tired.
Sono contento che vengano.I'm glad they're coming.

Impersonal expressions

Necessity, possibility, quality judgements.

È necessario che tutti partecipino.It's necessary that everyone take part.
Bisogna che io parta presto.I need to leave early.

After conjunctions

A fixed list always takes the congiuntivo.

Benché sia tardi, continuo.Although it's late, I'm carrying on.
Te lo dico affinché tu capisca.I'm telling you so that you understand.
Esco, a meno che non piova.I'll go out unless it rains.

Traps

Certainty takes the indicative

If the main clause states a fact rather than an opinion, no subjunctive.

So che sia arrivato.So che è arrivato. (I know.) · Credo che sia arrivato. (I believe.)

Same subject: use the infinitive

Both clauses have the same subject: di + infinitive.

Penso che io abbia ragione.Penso di avere ragione.

Ambiguous forms

Io, tu and lui look the same, so say who you mean.

Spero che stia bene. (who?)Spero che tu stia bene.

Compare

vs Congiuntivo passato

Present: the same moment or later. Passato: already finished before the main verb.

vs Presente

The indicative states a fact; the congiuntivo marks it as a view.

Condizionale

Condizionale passato

Past conditionalB1
avere or essere in the condizionale presente + past participle

What would have happened but did not, regrets, and the “future in the past”.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

It has two uses, and the second catches almost every English speaker. The first is straightforward: what would have happened but did not (Sarei venuto, ma non stavo bene).

The second is the future seen from the past: when you report, in the past, what someone said would happen. English says “he said he would come”; Italian does not use the present conditional here, it uses the past conditional: Ha detto che sarebbe venuto. It feels wrong for a long time before it feels right.

It is also the form for regrets and softened criticism: Avrei dovuto chiedere prima (I should have asked earlier), Avrei voluto aiutarti (I would have liked to help).

How to build it

  1. Take the condizionale presente of the auxiliaryavrei, avresti, avrebbe, avremmo, avreste, avrebbero · sarei, saresti, sarebbe, saremmo, sareste, sarebbero
  2. Add the past participleAgree with the subject when using essere.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioavrei mangiatosarei andato / andata
tuavresti mangiatosaresti andato / andata
lui / leiavrebbe mangiatosarebbe andato / andata
noiavremmo mangiatosaremmo andati / andate
voiavreste mangiatosareste andati / andate
loroavrebbero mangiatosarebbero andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioavreisarei
tuavrestisaresti
lui / leiavrebbesarebbe
noiavremmosaremmo
voiavrestesareste
loroavrebberosarebbero

Uses

What would have happened

Usually the result clause after se + congiuntivo trapassato.

Sarei venuto, ma non stavo bene.I would have come, but I wasn't well.
Se avessi saputo, avrei detto di sì.If I had known, I would have said yes.

Regret and should have

Dovere and potere.

Avrei dovuto chiedere prima.I should have asked earlier.
Avresti potuto avvisarmi.You could have warned me.

Future in the past

Reporting a plan or an expectation after a past verb.

Ha detto che sarebbe venuto.He said he would come.
Sapevo che non avrebbe funzionato.I knew it wouldn't work.

Traps

Future in the past is not the present conditional

After a past main verb, the reported future takes the condizionale passato.

Ha detto che verrebbe.Ha detto che sarebbe venuto.

Wrong tense in the se clause

The se clause takes the congiuntivo trapassato.

Se avrei saputo, sarei venuto.Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto.

Compare

vs Condizionale presente

Presente: would. Passato: would have.

vs Congiuntivo trapassato

The partner of the hypothesis.

Indicativo

Passato remoto

Historic past · preteriteB2
stem + ai / ei / ii · many irregulars, almost always in io, lui and loro

A completed past with no felt link to the present: the tense of novels, history and narration, and of everyday speech in much of the south.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

In practice this is the tense of literature, history and narrative, and of everyday speech across much of southern Italy, where it replaces the passato prossimo entirely. In the north it is read far more than it is spoken. For a learner the priority is clear: you need to recognise it fluently, because it fills novels, news features and history writing, but you rarely need to produce it.

The regular forms are simple. The irregular ones follow one reliable rule: they are irregular in only three persons, io, lui/lei and loro (the “1-3-6” pattern). The other three, tu, noi, voi, are regular, built on the infinitive stem: scrivere → scrissi, scrivesti, scrisse, scrivemmo, scriveste, scrissero.

The commonest irregular verbs follow a handful of shapes: the -si type (scrissi, chiusi, presi), and the -i with stem change type (ebbi, seppi, vidi, venni).

How to build it

  1. Take the stemparl-, cred-, dorm-
  2. Add the endings for the group-are: -ai, -asti, -ò, -ammo, -aste, -arono · -ere: -ei (-etti), -esti, -é (-ette), -emmo, -este, -erono (-ettero) · -ire: -ii, -isti, -ì, -immo, -iste, -irono
  3. For the irregular verbs, change io, lui, loro onlyLearn the io form; lui is the same with -e (scrisse), loro with -ero (scrissero). Tu, noi, voi stay regular.

Endings

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

-areparlare-erecredere-iredormire

tuparlasticredestidormisti

voiparlastecredestedormiste
loroparlaronocrederonodormirono

Many -ere verbs have a second io / lui / loro form in -etti, -ette, -ettero (credetti, credette, credettero). Both are correct.

Irregulars

There are many irregular verbs here, but the rule is stable: irregular in io, lui, loro, regular in tu, noi, voi. The table shows the three irregular persons in colour. A few, such as essere, avere, fare, dare, stare, are irregular in every person.

Uses

History and biography

Events completed and closed in the distant past.

Fondarono lo studio nel 1985.They founded the studio in 1985.
Dante nacque a Firenze.Dante was born in Florence.

Narration in writing

Novels, short stories, formal reports.

Lesse la lettera e uscì.He read the letter and went out.
Aprì la porta e vide il mare.She opened the door and saw the sea.

Everyday speech in the south

Where speakers use it for last year, last month, even yesterday.

Ieri andai al mercato.Yesterday I went to the market. (southern usage)

Traps

Do not use it for “this morning” or “today”

It implies the period is over and distant, so with oggi / stamattina / quest'anno prefer the passato prossimo.

Stamattina mangiai un panino.Stamattina ho mangiato un panino.

Irregular in three persons only

Do not irregularise tu, noi, voi.

Tu scrissi. · Noi scrissimo.Tu scrivesti. · Noi scrivemmo.

Compare

vs Passato prossimo

Same meaning, different register and region. Production: passato prossimo. Recognition: both.

vs Imperfetto

The remoto narrates the events, the imperfetto still describes the scene: Pioveva quando uscì.

Congiuntivo

Congiuntivo passato

Past subjunctiveB2
avere or essere in the congiuntivo presente + past participle

Same triggers as the present subjunctive, but the action in the subordinate clause is already complete.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The same triggers as the present subjunctive, but the subordinate action is earlier than the main verb. The main clause is in the present (or future), and the subordinate action is already done: Credo che abbiano già deciso.

It is built the usual way, with the same auxiliary as in the passato prossimo, so there is no new decision to make, only the subjunctive of the auxiliary: abbia, abbia, abbia, abbiamo, abbiate, abbiano · sia, sia, sia, siamo, siate, siano.

How to build it

  1. Take the congiuntivo presente of the auxiliaryabbia, abbia, abbia, abbiamo, abbiate, abbiano · sia, sia, sia, siamo, siate, siano
  2. Add the past participleAgree with the subject when using essere.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare

loroabbiano mangiatosiano andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioabbiasia
tuabbiasia
lui / leiabbiasia
noiabbiamosiamo
voiabbiatesiate
loroabbianosiano

Uses

A completed action seen from the present

Main verb present, subordinate action finished.

Credo che abbiano già deciso.I believe they have already decided.
Mi dispiace che sia andata così.I'm sorry it went that way.
Sembra che siano partiti ieri.It seems they left yesterday.

After conjunctions about a completed action

Benché, sebbene, nonostante.

Benché abbia studiato molto, non ha passato l'esame.Although he studied a lot, he didn't pass the exam.

Traps

Present instead of passato

If the action happened before, the present is wrong.

Credo che lui parte ieri.Credo che lui sia partito ieri.

Indicative after a doubt

Doubt or opinion still needs the congiuntivo.

Penso che ha capito.Penso che abbia capito.

Compare

vs Congiuntivo presente

Presente: simultaneous or future. Passato: before.

vs Passato prossimo

The indicative equivalent of this tense is the passato prossimo.

Congiuntivo

Congiuntivo imperfetto

Imperfect subjunctiveB2
stem + assi · assi · asse · assimo · aste · assero (-are) · essi… (-ere) · issi… (-ire)

The subjunctive for the past, and the tense of the unreal “if” clause. Regular, and used constantly in real conversation.

ExplanationHow to build itEndingsIrregularsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

It has two jobs. First, it is the past-tense subjunctive: when the main verb moves into the past (or the conditional), the subjunctive in the subordinate clause moves with it. Penso che sia facile → Pensavo che fosse facile.

Second, and more important in everyday speech, it is the tense of the unreal condition: Se avessi più tempo, studierei di più. Learners often avoid it, which is a mistake: it is one of the most-used tenses in real conversation and it is remarkably regular.

It also follows come se (as if), magari and many wishes (Magari fosse vero!), and expressions such as vorrei che… and sarebbe meglio che….

How to build it

  1. Take the stem from the infinitiveparl-, cred-, dorm-
  2. Add -assi / -essi / -issiparlassi, parlassi, parlasse, parlassimo, parlaste, parlassero. The group vowel (a/e/i) is followed by -ssi.
  3. The irregulars are fewessere → fossi · fare → facessi · dire → dicessi · bere → bevessi · dare → dessi · stare → stessi

Endings

Grey is the stem, bold is what the tense adds.

-areparlare-erecredere-iredormire
ioparlassicredessidormissi
tuparlassicredessidormissi
lui / leiparlassecredessedormisse
noiparlassimocredessimodormissimo
voiparlastecredestedormiste
loroparlasserocredesserodormissero

Irregulars

Almost perfectly regular: only the verbs that keep their longer stem (fare, dire, bere, essere, dare, stare and the -rre verbs) differ.

verbiotului / leinoivoiloro
bereto drinkbevessibevessibevessebevessimobevestebevessero
dareto givedessidessidessedessimodestedessero
direto say / telldicessidicessidicessedicessimodicestedicessero
essereto befossifossifossefossimofostefossero
fareto do / to makefacessifacessifacessefacessimofacestefacessero
stareto stay / to bestessistessistessestessimostestestessero

The -rre verbs (11 verbs)

Contracted from Latin (tradurre ← traducere): they use the long stem (traduc-, pon-, trae-) everywhere except where the contracted form is built from the infinitive.

verbiotului / leinoivoiloro
attrarreto attractattraessiattraessiattraesseattraessimoattraesteattraessero
comporreto composecomponessicomponessicomponessecomponessimocomponestecomponessero
condurreto lead / conductconducessiconducessiconducesseconducessimoconducesteconducessero
distrarreto distractdistraessidistraessidistraessedistraessimodistraestedistraessero

imporreto imposeimponessiimponessiimponesseimponessimoimponesteimponessero
introdurreto introduceintroducessiintroducessiintroducesseintroducessimointroducesteintroducessero
produrreto produceproducessiproducessiproducesseproducessimoproducesteproducessero

Uses

The past version of the subjunctive

Main verb in a past tense or the conditional.

Pensavo che fosse più semplice.I thought it was simpler.
Speravo che tu venissi.I was hoping you'd come.
Vorrei che tu venissi.I'd like you to come.

The “if” clause of an unreal present or future

Followed by the condizionale presente.

Se avessi più tempo, studierei di più.If I had more time, I'd study more.
Se fossi in te, accetterei.If I were you, I'd accept.

After come se

As if, always imperfetto or trapassato.

Parla come se sapesse tutto.He talks as if he knew everything.

Wishes

With magari.

Magari fosse vero!If only it were true!

Traps

Never se + condizionale

The se clause takes the congiuntivo. The conditional goes in the other half.

Se avrei tempo, studierei.Se avessi tempo, studierei.

Do not confuse with the passato remoto

Parlassi (subjunctive) is not parlai (remoto).

Se io parlai meglio…Se io parlassi meglio…

Compare

vs Congiuntivo presente

Sequence of tenses: main verb present → congiuntivo presente; main verb past or conditional → congiuntivo imperfetto.

vs Condizionale presente

They work as a pair in the hypothesis: Se avessi tempo (cgim), studierei (cond).

Congiuntivo

Congiuntivo trapassato

Pluperfect subjunctiveB2
avere or essere in the congiuntivo imperfetto + past participle

The impossible hypothesis, the regret, and the earlier action seen from the past.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The condition that was not met, and now cannot be: Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto. This is the tense of regret and it pairs with the condizionale passato in the other half of the sentence.

It is also the congiuntivo form for an action that was completed before a past main verb: Credevo che fossero già partiti. And it follows come se when the comparison is about the past: Mi guardava come se non mi avesse mai visto.

How to build it

  1. Take the congiuntivo imperfetto of the auxiliaryavessi, avessi, avesse, avessimo, aveste, avessero · fossi, fossi, fosse, fossimo, foste, fossero
  2. Add the past participleAgree with the subject when using essere.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioavessi mangiatofossi andato / andata
tuavessi mangiatofossi andato / andata
lui / leiavesse mangiatofosse andato / andata
noiavessimo mangiatofossimo andati / andate
voiaveste mangiatofoste andati / andate
loroavessero mangiatofossero andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioavessifossi
tuavessifossi
lui / leiavessefosse
noiavessimofossimo
voiavestefoste
loroavesserofossero

Uses

The impossible hypothesis in the past

If it had been different… it would have been different.

Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto.If I had known, I would have come.
Se fossimo partiti prima, avremmo preso il treno.If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.

Regret and wishes about the past

Magari, vorrei che.

Magari avessi studiato di più!If only I'd studied more!

Earlier than a past main verb

Sequence of tenses.

Credevo che fossero già partiti.I thought they had already left.
Non sapevo che avesse cambiato idea.I didn't know he had changed his mind.

Mixed hypothesis

Past cause, present effect.

Se avessi studiato, ora saprei.If I had studied, I would know now.

Traps

Conditional in the se clause

Same rule as the imperfetto: not after se.

Se sarei venuto, ti avrei visto.Se fossi venuto, ti avrei visto.

Double conditional

Only the result half takes the condizionale.

Se avrei saputo, sarei venuto.Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto.

Compare

vs Congiuntivo imperfetto

Imperfetto: unreal now / future. Trapassato: unreal past.

vs Condizionale passato

It is the partner clause: Se avessi saputo (cgt), sarei venuto (cond. passato).

Indicativo

Trapassato remoto

Past anteriorC1
avere or essere in the passato remoto + past participle

The rarest tense in the language. Written, literary, and only in a clause with dopo che / appena. Recognise it and move on.

ExplanationHow to build itModelUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

It appears exclusively in writing, in a subordinate clause introduced by dopo che, appena, quando, finché non, and only when the main clause is in the passato remoto. The speaker or narrator places an event as completed immediately before another past event. In speech the passato prossimo or trapassato prossimo does the same job.

You will meet it in older novels and in some historical writing. You do not need to produce it for B2.

How to build it

  1. Take the passato remoto of the auxiliaryebbi, avesti, ebbe, avemmo, aveste, ebbero · fui, fosti, fu, fummo, foste, furono
  2. Add the past participleAgree with the subject when the auxiliary is essere.

Model

The auxiliary carries the tense; the participle carries the meaning. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (masculine -o / -i, feminine -a / -e).

avere + participle mangiareessere + participle andare
ioebbi mangiatofui andato / andata
tuavesti mangiatofosti andato / andata
lui / leiebbe mangiatofu andato / andata
noiavemmo mangiatofummo andati / andate
voiaveste mangiatofoste andati / andate
loroebbero mangiatofurono andati / andate
The auxiliary on its own (avere and essere in the tense used here)
avere for most verbsessere motion · change · reflexive
ioebbifui
tuavestifosti
lui / leiebbefu
noiavemmofummo
voiavestefoste
loroebberofurono

Uses

A completed event immediately before another past event

Always paired with a main clause in the passato remoto.

Dopo che ebbe finito, uscì.After he had finished, he went out.
Appena furono partiti, cominciò a piovere.As soon as they had left, it started to rain.

Traps

Do not use it in speech

Its modern equivalents are the trapassato prossimo or just the passato prossimo.

Dopo che ebbi mangiato, sono uscito.Dopo che ho mangiato, sono uscito. · Dopo aver mangiato, sono uscito.

Compare

vs Trapassato prossimo

Same idea, everyday register: Dopo che aveva finito, è uscito.

Test yourself

Conjugate any verb in this tense in the verb library →
← Congiuntivo trapassato
Periphrasis

Progressive (stare + gerund)

Present continuous · "I am doing"A2
stare (presente, imperfetto, futuro, condizionale) + gerund · sto parlando, stavo parlando, starò parlando

What English calls the present continuous. Italian has it too, but uses it less: it says "I am in the middle of doing this, right now".

ExplanationHow to build itFormsUsesTrapsCompareTest

Explanation

The progressive is not a tense of its own. It is a periphrasis: the verb stare, in whatever tense you need, followed by the gerund of the action. That is why it is not one of the fifteen forms, but it is one of the first things an English speaker reaches for, so it deserves a page.

Italian uses the plain presente for far more than English uses the present continuous. "I work in Milan" and "I am working today" can both be lavoro. Use sto lavorando only when you want to stress that the action is in progress at this very moment, or temporary.

The same logic works one tense back: stavo lavorando is "I was in the middle of working" when something interrupted: Stavo lavorando quando è arrivato Marco.

How to build it

  1. Choose the tense of starePresente for now, imperfetto for a past action in progress, futuro for "will be doing" (rare), condizionale for "would be doing".
  2. Form the gerund-are → -ando · -ere / -ire → -endo. The gerund never changes for person, gender or number.
  3. Join themSto + parlando = sto parlando. The subject pronoun is optional, as always.
  4. Place the pronounsBefore stare, or attached to the gerund: lo sto leggendo or sto leggendolo. Reflexives work the same: mi sto lavando / sto lavandomi.

Forms

First, stare in the four tenses you will use with it.

PresenteImperfettoFuturoCondizionale
iostostavostaròstarei
tustaistavistaraistaresti
lui / lei / Leistastavastaràstarebbe
noistiamostavamostaremostaremmo
voistatestavatestaretestareste
lorostannostavanostarannostarebbero

Then the gerund.

InfinitiveGerund
parlareparlando
mangiaremangiando
crederecredendo
scriverescrivendo
dormiredormendo
finirefinendo
Irregular: the stem keeps the old, longer form
farefacendo
diredicendo
berebevendo
porreponendo
trarretraendo
produrreproducendo
tradurretraducendo

Uses

An action in progress right now

The action has started and has not finished.

Sto scrivendo un'email.I am writing an email.
Che cosa stai facendo?What are you doing?
Stiamo aspettando il treno.We are waiting for the train.

An action in progress in the past

Use stare in the imperfetto, usually with an interruption.

Stavo guardando un film quando hai chiamato.I was watching a film when you called.
Stavamo uscendo quando è iniziato a piovere.We were going out when it started to rain.

Temporary situations

Something true for now, not as a general rule.

Questa settimana sto lavorando da casa.This week I am working from home.
Sto imparando l'italiano.I am learning Italian.

About to: stare per + infinitive

A different structure that looks similar. It means "on the point of".

Sto per uscire.I am about to go out.
Il treno sta per partire.The train is about to leave.

Traps

Not for the future

English says "I am leaving tomorrow". Italian uses the plain presente or the futuro.

Domani sto partendo per Roma.Domani parto per Roma.

The verb is stare, not essere

Essere + gerund does not exist in Italian.

Sono mangiando.Sto mangiando.

Not for habits or general truths

A routine is the plain presente.

Di solito sto bevendo il caffè alle otto.Di solito bevo il caffè alle otto.

Not with verbs of state

Verbs of knowing, wanting, liking and being take the plain tense.

Sto sapendo la risposta.So la risposta.

Do not add a gerund ending to the wrong stem

Fare, dire and bere keep the longer stem.

Sto farendo i compiti.Sto facendo i compiti.

Compare

Presente vs progressivo. Both are correct for an action happening now. The presente is neutral: Che fai? The progressive asks about this exact moment: Che stai facendo?. For a plan or a routine, only the presente works.

Imperfetto vs stavo + gerund. The imperfetto describes a habit or background; stavo + gerund puts one action under a spotlight, usually when another one interrupts it.
