Italian grammar reference · Section 4

Choosing between them, which is the harder half

Knowing fourteen tenses is not the same as knowing which one a sentence needs. This section covers the contrasts that decide most sentences, the three types of conditional, and the rule that matches a subordinate clause to its main verb.

Prossimo or imperfettoProssimo or remotoTrapassato or condizionaleThe two futuresPeriodo ipoteticoConcordanzaIndicativo or congiuntivoTest yourself

Passato prossimo or imperfetto

The big one

This is the single most consequential choice in Italian past narration, and it is not about how long ago something happened. It is about whether you are reporting an event or describing a situation.

THE EVENT

Passato prossimo

Something happened. It had a beginning and an end. It moves the story forward.

Ieri ho finito il progetto.
Yesterday I finished the project.

Ha chiamato due volte.
He called twice.

THE FRAME

Imperfetto

How things were. Habits, descriptions, states, and actions in progress. It sets the scene.

Ogni giorno finivo alle sei.
Every day I used to finish at six.

Era stanco e non voleva parlare.
He was tired and didn't want to talk.

The test: ask whether you are saying what happened or how things were. Events take the passato prossimo. Everything that frames them takes the imperfetto. In one sentence: Mentre lavoravo (frame), è arrivato il cliente (event).

Six verbs that change meaning with the tense

IMPERFETTO — THE STATE  ·  PASSATO PROSSIMO — THE MOMENT IT CHANGED
sapevo — I knewho saputo — I found out
conoscevo — I knew (was acquainted with)ho conosciuto — I met (for the first time)
volevo — I wanted toho voluto — I insisted, and did it
non volevo — I didn't want tonon ho voluto — I refused
dovevo — I was supposed toho dovuto — I had to, and did
potevo — I was able toho potuto — I managed to

These six are worth memorising as pairs. They are frequently tested, and getting one wrong does not sound slightly off — it changes what you said.

Passato prossimo or passato remoto

Not a grammar choice so much as a question of register and geography.

SPEECH, AND MOST WRITING

Passato prossimo

The default across the country in conversation, email and journalism. Standard everywhere.

Ho vissuto a Roma per tre anni.
I lived in Rome for three years.

LITERATURE, HISTORY, THE SOUTH

Passato remoto

Distant, closed past. Standard in narrative writing, and normal in everyday speech in much of the south.

Visse a Roma per tre anni.
He lived in Rome for three years.

Practical advice: produce the passato prossimo, recognise the passato remoto. You will read it constantly and rarely need to write it — but if you plan to live in the south, expect to hear it in conversation.

Trapassato prossimo or condizionale passato

Commonly confused

Both translate into English with had or would have, and both are compound. The difference is whether the thing actually happened.

IT HAPPENED

Trapassato prossimo

A real past event, placed before another past event. Auxiliary in the imperfetto.

Avevo già finito quando è arrivato.
I had already finished when he arrived.

IT DID NOT HAPPEN

Condizionale passato

Usually an unrealised past: what would have been, but was not. It can also report a future seen from the past: Disse che sarebbe partito. Auxiliary in the conditional.

Avrei finito, ma è arrivato.
I would have finished, but he arrived.

The test: did it actually occur? Avevo finito means the work was done. Avrei finito usually means it was not (it can also report a plan seen from the past: Disse che avrebbe finito). The auxiliary carries the entire difference, so listen for avevo against avrei.

Futuro semplice or futuro anteriore

THE ACTION ITSELF

Futuro semplice

Something that will happen. Also a guess about the present.

Ti chiamo quando finisco.
I'll call you when I finish.

Sarà in riunione.
He must be in a meeting.

FINISHED FIRST

Futuro anteriore

Completed before another future point. Also a guess about the past.

Quando avrò finito, ti chiamo.
When I've finished, I'll call you.

Avrà dimenticato.
He must have forgotten.

Note: in everyday speech the present very often replaces both — quando finisco, ti chiamo is entirely normal. The compound future is more common in writing.

Il periodo ipotetico — the three types of if

Core B2

Italian sorts conditional sentences into three patterns by how likely the condition is. Each one fixes both halves of the sentence, so once you identify the type, both verbs are decided for you.

Type 1 · Reality

The condition is likely or real

se + indicativo presente  →  indicativo presente or futuro

Se piove, resto a casa.If it rains, I'll stay at home.
Se hai tempo, ti mando il file.If you have time, I'll send you the file.
Type 2 · Possibility

The condition is imagined or unlikely

se + congiuntivo imperfetto  →  condizionale presente

Se avessi più tempo, studierei di più.If I had more time, I would study more.
Se fossi in te, accetterei.If I were you, I would accept.
Type 3 · Impossibility

The condition was not met and now cannot be

se + congiuntivo trapassato  →  condizionale passato

Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto.If I had known, I would have come.
Se avessimo cominciato prima, avremmo finito.If we had started earlier, we would have finished.

Mixed time frames are allowed

A past condition can have a present result: Se avessi studiato, ora saprei. If I had studied, I would know now.

No conditional after se in an if-clause

The conditional belongs in the result clause only. The if-clause takes the indicative or the subjunctive, never the conditional. (Se also introduces indirect questions, where the conditional can be right: Mi chiedo se sarebbe possibile.)

Se avrei tempo, studierei.Se avessi tempo, studierei.

Concordanza dei tempi — matching the subordinate clause

Exam material

Once a subjunctive trigger is in place, the tense of the main verb decides which subjunctive you need. This table is standard exam material and it removes most of the guesswork.

MAIN CLAUSE IN THE PRESENT — PENSO CHE…
…sia difficile…it is difficult — congiuntivo presente, same time
…sia stato difficile…it was difficult — congiuntivo passato, earlier
…sarà difficile…it will be difficult — indicativo futuro, later
MAIN CLAUSE IN THE PAST — PENSAVO CHE…
…fosse difficile…it was difficult — congiuntivo imperfetto, same time
…fosse stato difficile…it had been difficult — congiuntivo trapassato, earlier
…sarebbe stato difficile…it would be difficult — condizionale passato, later

The last line is the one to memorise. After a past main verb, a later action takes the condizionale passato, not the present conditional. Pensavo che sarebbe venuto.

These pages explain the tenses. They do not conjugate them.

For the full conjugation of any verb in any of these tenses — all six persons, 342 verbs including the reflexives — go to the verb library. It can be filtered the other way round too: choose one tense and see every verb in it at once.

Open the verb library →

Indicativo or congiuntivo — deciding in one step

The subjunctive is not about difficulty or formality. It is mostly about whether the subordinate clause is presented as a fact or as a view, wish or doubt. Some triggers take it even for true facts (benché, mi dispiace che).

YOU ARE STATING A FACT

Indicativo

After verbs of knowing, seeing and saying — anything presented as true.

So che è arrivato.
I know he has arrived.

È vero che costa molto.
It's true that it costs a lot.

Dico che funziona.
I say it works.

YOU ARE NOT

Congiuntivo

After opinion, doubt, emotion, hope, will, fear — and after benché, purché, prima che, affinché, senza che.

Credo che sia arrivato.
I believe he has arrived.

Dubito che costi molto.
I doubt it costs a lot.

Voglio che funzioni.
I want it to work.

Two exceptions worth knowing: anche se is close to benché and normally takes the indicative for something real (Anche se piove, esco); with the congiuntivo imperfetto it becomes hypothetical (Anche se piovesse, uscirei). And direi che takes the indicative, because the conditional has already done the hedging.

Italian grammar reference · Section 5

The words that point, replace and connect

Demonstratives, relatives, possessives and object pronouns. These are the words that let you stop repeating the noun — and the ones whose placement most clearly marks a learner from a speaker.

Questo & quelloChe & cuiQuestionsPossessivesObject pronounsStressedIndefinitesTest yourself

Questo and quello

Two words, seven forms

This one is close to the speaker, that one is not. Questo behaves like any four-form adjective. Quello copies the definite article, which is why it has seven forms.

questo — near me

questo progetto · questa riunione · questi file · queste note
this project · this meeting · these files · these notes

quello — over there

Take the article the noun would use and rebuild it:
il → quel · lo → quello · l' → quell' · la → quella
i → quei · gli → quegli · le → quelle
IN USE
quel cliente · quello studio · quell'ufficiothat client · that studio · that office
quella proposta · quei documentithat proposal · those documents
quegli appunti · quelle stampethose notes · those prints
STANDING ALONE, QUELLO IS SIMPLE AGAIN
Preferisco questo, non quello.I prefer this one, not that one.
Quelle sono le mie.Those are mine.

ciò is the invariable neuter version of quello — it means "that thing" and never changes: Ciò che dici è vero. — What you say is true.

Che, cui, il quale

Never omitted

Italian joins two clauses with a relative pronoun far more often than English, which can drop it. In Italian it is never optional.

che — subject or direct object

One word, no gender, no number, no preposition.
Il cliente che ha chiamato. The client who called.
Il file che ho mandato. The file (that) I sent.

cui — after a preposition

Whenever a preposition is needed, che becomes cui.
Il progetto di cui parlo. The project I'm talking about.
La persona a cui ho scritto. The person I wrote to.
CUI WITH EACH PREPOSITION
il tema di cui discutiamothe topic we're discussing
il collega a cui ho chiestothe colleague I asked
l'anno in cui sono arrivatothe year I arrived
lo studio con cui lavorothe studio I work with
il motivo per cui ho sceltothe reason I chose
il libro da cui ho imparatothe book I learned from
IL CUI = WHOSE
il cliente il cui progetto è stato approvatothe client whose project was approved
l'azienda i cui uffici sono a Milanothe company whose offices are in Milan

English drops it, Italian cannot

In English "the file I sent" is fine. In Italian the relative pronoun must appear.

Il file ho mandato.Il file che ho mandato.

il quale — the formal alternative

il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali can replace che or cui in writing, and they carry gender, which removes ambiguity.
La collega della quale ti parlavo. The colleague I was telling you about.

Asking questions

chiwho — the word never changes; the verb is usually singular (Chi è arrivato?), plural only when the predicate is (Chi siete?)
che · che cosa · cosawhat — all three are correct, cosa is the most spoken
quale · qualiwhich — agrees in number
quanto · quanta · quanti · quantehow much · how many — agrees fully
come · dove · quando · perchéhow · where · when · why
IN USE
Chi ha preparato il documento?Who prepared the document?
Cosa ne pensi?What do you think about it?
Quale versione preferisci?Which version do you prefer?
Quante persone vengono?How many people are coming?

qual è is written without an apostrophe. Qual è il problema? — never qual'è. This is a common written error even among native speakers.

Possessives

One exception

Italian possessives normally keep the definite article, which surprises English speakers. There is one clean exception.

il mio · la mia · i miei · le miemy
il tuo · la tua · i tuoi · le tueyour (informal)
il suo · la sua · i suoi · le suehis · her · its — and your, formal
il nostro · la nostra · i nostri · le nostreour
il vostro · la vostra · i vostri · le vostreyour (plural)
il loro · la loro · i loro · le lorotheir — loro never changes

The article stays

Il mio progetto è finito. My project is finished.
Ho perso le mie note. I lost my notes.

Except with a single family member

Drop the article for one relative, singular and unmodified. Bring it back for plurals or with an adjective.

mio padre · mia sorella · mio fratelloi miei genitori · le mie sorelle — plural takes the article backil mio fratello maggiore · mio fratello maggiore — both are heard; the article is more usual with an adjectiveil loro padre — loro always keeps the article

The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not the owner. la sua macchina is "his car" or "her car" — the form follows macchina.

Object pronouns

High frequency

These replace a noun already known. Direct objects answer what, indirect objects answer to whom.

Direct — what

mi · ti · lo · la · ci · vi · li · le
Hai visto il file? Sì, l'ho visto. Have you seen the file? Yes, I've seen it.

Indirect — to whom

mi · ti · gli · le · ci · vi · gli
Hai scritto a Marco? Sì, gli ho scritto. Have you written to Marco? Yes, I've written to him.
WHERE THE PRONOUN GOES
Lo conosco bene.I know him well. — before a conjugated verb
Voglio vederlo. · Lo voglio vedere.I want to see him. — either place with a modal
Dimmi tutto. · Non dirmelo.Tell me everything. · Don't tell me. — attached to the imperative
Le ho parlato ieri.I spoke to her yesterday.
AGREEMENT IN THE PASSATO PROSSIMO
Le stampe? Le ho viste.The prints? I've seen them. — participle agrees with lo, la, li, le
Ho visto le stampe.I've seen the prints. — no pronoun, no agreement

Combined pronouns

When both appear, the indirect comes first and its i becomes e.
mi + lo → me lo · ti + lo → te lo · ci + lo → ce lo · vi + lo → ve lo
gli/le + lo → glielo — one word, for him and for her alike

In use

Me lo mandi domani? Will you send it to me tomorrow?
Gliel'ho già detto. I've already told him. / told her.
Te ne parlo dopo. I'll tell you about it later.

Stressed pronouns

Used after a preposition, or when you want emphasis. These are the forms that survive on their own.

me · te · lui · lei · noi · voi · lorome · you · him · her · us · you · them
WHERE THEY APPEAR
Vieni con me.Come with me. — always after a preposition
Questo è per te.This is for you.
Ha scelto lei, non io.She chose, not me. — emphasis
Secondo me, funziona.In my opinion, it works.

Indefinites

Two traps

Small words for unspecified quantity. Two of them force a singular noun, which is where the errors live.

qualcuno · qualcosasomeone · something
ognuno · ognieach one · every
tutto · tutti · tutteeverything · everyone · all
alcuni · alcune · qualchesome, a few
nessuno · niente · nullanobody · nothing
altro · altri · un altroother · others · another

qualche is always followed by a singular noun

It means "some" but takes the singular form, unlike alcuni.

qualche giorniqualche giorno · alcuni giorni — both mean "a few days"

ogni is invariable and singular too

It never takes a plural and never changes form.

ogni giorni · ogni le settimaneogni giorno · ogni settimana

Negatives need non before the verb

If the negative word comes after the verb, non is required in front of it.

Nessuno è venuto is fine, but: Ho visto nessuno.Non ho visto nessuno. · Non c'è niente.

qualcosa takes di before an adjective

qualcosa di interessante something interesting
niente di nuovo nothing new

Italian grammar reference · Section 6

Adverbs, and where they belong

Most adverbs are built from an adjective with one suffix. The difficulty is not forming them — it is knowing when a word is acting as an adjective and when as an adverb, and where in the sentence it goes.

FormationIrregular pairsQuantityFrequency & timePlace & mannerPositionTest yourself

Turning an adjective into an adverb

One rule, two shortcuts

One suffix does most of the work. Take the feminine singular of the adjective and add -mente.

THE BASIC RULE — FEMININE FORM + MENTE
lento → lenta → lentamenteslow → slowly
chiaro → chiara → chiaramenteclear → clearly
preciso → precisa → precisamenteprecise → precisely
raro → rara → raramenterare → rarely
ADJECTIVES ENDING IN -E ADD MENTE DIRECTLY
veloce → velocementefast → quickly
recente → recentementerecent → recently
ADJECTIVES IN -LE OR -RE PRECEDED BY A VOWEL DROP THE FINAL E (exception: acre → acremente)
facile → facilmenteeasy → easily
difficile → difficilmentedifficult → hardly, with difficulty
regolare → regolarmenteregular → regularly
particolare → particolarmenteparticular → particularly

The pairs that do not follow it

Memorise these

Four adjectives have their own adverb, and mixing them up is one of the most audible learner errors.

Adjective → adverb

buono → bene good → well
cattivo → male bad → badly
migliore → meglio better (adj) → better (adv)
peggiore → peggio worse (adj) → worse (adv)

An adjective describes a noun, an adverb describes a verb

buono modifies a thing; bene modifies an action.

Il caffè è bene. · Parlo buono l'italiano.Il caffè è buono. — the coffee is goodParlo bene l'italiano. — I speak Italian well

Sto bene means "I am well" — with stare, always the adverb. Sono buono would mean "I am a good person".

Quantity

Agree or not

These four change form as adjectives but never change as adverbs. Deciding which role they are playing is the whole trick.

AS AN ADVERB — MODIFYING A VERB OR ADJECTIVE, INVARIABLE
Lavoro molto.I work a lot.
È molto interessante.It's very interesting.
Ho dormito poco.I slept little.
Parla troppo.He talks too much.
AS AN ADJECTIVE — MODIFYING A NOUN, AGREES
Ho molto lavoro. · Ho molte riunioni.I have a lot of work. · I have many meetings.
Ho poco tempo. · Ho poche idee.I have little time. · I have few ideas.
Troppi file, troppe cartelle.Too many files, too many folders.
THE INVARIABLE ONES
abbastanzaenough, quite — never changes
piuttostorather
quasialmost

Frequency and time

HOW OFTEN
sempre · di solito · spessoalways · usually · often
qualche volta · a volte · raramentesometimes · at times · rarely
mai · non ... maiever · never — after the verb you need non … mai (Non lo faccio mai); with mai first you drop non (Mai lo farei)
ancora · non ... ancorastill · not yet
già · non ... piùalready · not any more
WHEN
adesso · ora · subitonow · now · immediately
prima · dopo · poibefore · after · then
presto · tardi · in ritardoearly · late · late (behind schedule)
appenajust, as soon as — Sono appena arrivato.
oggi · ieri · domanitoday · yesterday · tomorrow
stamattina · stasera · stanottethis morning · this evening · tonight

Place and manner

Place

qui · qua here · lì · là there
sopra · sotto above · below · dentro · fuori inside · outside
davanti · dietro in front · behind · vicino · lontano near · far
dappertutto everywhere · altrove elsewhere

Manner

bene · male well · badly · così like this
insieme together · piano slowly, quietly · forte loudly, hard
volentieri gladly · apposta on purpose · di nuovo again

Where the adverb sits

Position matters

Position is not free. Three placements cover almost every case.

AFTER THE VERB — THE DEFAULT
Parlo lentamente.I speak slowly.
Lavora bene.He works well.
BETWEEN THE AUXILIARY AND THE PARTICIPLE
Ho già finito.I've already finished.
Non ho ancora deciso.I haven't decided yet.
Non sono mai stato in Italia.I have never been to Italy.
Ho sempre lavorato così.I have always worked this way.
AT THE FRONT — FOR EMPHASIS OR TIME
Di solito comincio alle nove.I usually start at nine.
Purtroppo non posso venire.Unfortunately I can't come.

Long adverbs usually follow the participle

Short adverbs (già, mai, ancora, sempre) go between auxiliary and participle; manner adverbs in -mente normally follow the participle.

Ho lentamente finito. (grammatical but marked: it puts the stress on the adverb)Ho finito lentamente.

anche goes before what it emphasises

Anche io lavoro qui. I work here too.
Lavoro anche il sabato. I work on Saturdays as well.

Italian grammar reference · Section 7

Connectors, and the ones that change the verb

The words that join clauses are easy to translate and hard to place. Several of them decide the mood of the verb that follows, which makes them grammar rather than vocabulary.

Joining ideasCause & consequenceTimeSubjunctive triggersTest yourself

Joining two ideas

e · anche · inoltreand · also · furthermore
ma · peròbut — però can also sit later in the sentence
o · oppureor
inveceinstead, whereas
anzion the contrary, in fact even more so
cioèthat is, in other words
infattiindeed, in fact — confirms what was just said
comunqueanyway, in any case
IN USE
Il progetto è pronto, però manca l'approvazione.The project is ready, but the approval is missing.
Non è tardi, anzi siamo in anticipo.It's not late — on the contrary, we're early.
Ci vediamo lunedì, cioè fra tre giorni.See you Monday, that is, in three days.

Cause and consequence

Word order rule

Italian distinguishes where the reason sits in the sentence. Perché cannot open a sentence in this sense; siccome and poiché can.

Cause — because

perché — never first in the sentence
siccome · dato che · visto che — normally first
poiché — formal, either position
grazie a · a causa di — before a noun, not a clause

Consequence — so

quindi · perciò · dunque therefore
allora so, then · così this way
di conseguenza consequently — formal
THE SAME SENTENCE, THREE WAYS
Non sono venuto perché ero malato.I didn't come because I was ill.
Siccome ero malato, non sono venuto.Since I was ill, I didn't come.
Ero malato, quindi non sono venuto.I was ill, so I didn't come.
BEFORE A NOUN, NOT A CLAUSE
Grazie al tuo aiuto, ho finito.Thanks to your help, I finished.
A causa del ritardo, abbiamo rimandato.Because of the delay, we postponed.

Prefer siccome or dato che at the start of a sentence

Causal perché normally follows the main clause. At the start of a sentence it sounds like the question “why?”, so use siccome or dato che instead (perché is fine in an answer: Perché ero malato.).

Perché ero malato, non sono venuto.Siccome ero malato, non sono venuto.

Time

Watch prima

Two of these carry a grammar consequence: prima che forces the subjunctive, and appena changes tense depending on whether it means "as soon as" or "just".

quandowhen
mentrewhile — two actions running together
appenaas soon as · just now
finché · finché nonas long as · until
ogni volta cheevery time that
dopo cheafter — followed by a full clause
prima chebefore — always followed by the subjunctive
IN USE
Mentre lavoravo, è arrivato il cliente.While I was working, the client arrived.
Appena arrivo, ti chiamo.As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.
Sono appena arrivato.I've just arrived.

prima che or prima di — decided by the subject

Different subjects take prima che plus the subjunctive. The same subject takes prima di plus the infinitive.

Prima che io esco, controllo tutto.Prima di uscire, controllo tutto. — same subject (the usual choice; prima che io esca is possible but heavy)Prima che tu esca, controlliamo tutto. — different subject

dopo works in a similar way

Same subject: dopo + past infinitive. Different subject: dopo che + a normal clause.
Dopo aver finito, sono uscito. After finishing, I went out.
Dopo che ha finito, siamo usciti. After he finished, we went out.

The connectors that force the subjunctive

Learn this table

This is the single most useful table in the section. If one of these words appears, the verb after it goes into the congiuntivo — no exceptions.

CONCESSION — ALTHOUGH
benché · sebbene · nonostante · malgradoalthough, even though — all take the subjunctive
anche seeven though — takes the INDICATIVE, not the subjunctive
CONDITION
purché · a patto che · a condizione cheprovided that
a meno che (non)unless
nel caso in cuiin case
PURPOSE
affinché · perché (meaning "so that")so that
per + infinitoin order to — no subjunctive, no subject change
TIME AND MANNER
prima chebefore
senza chewithout
come seas if — takes the imperfect subjunctive

With the subjunctive

Benché sia tardi, continuo a lavorare.
Although it's late, I keep working.

Ti aiuto, purché tu me lo chieda.
I'll help you, provided you ask me.

anche se is the exception

It means the same as benché but takes the indicative. This catches almost everyone.

Anche se sia tardi, continuo.Anche se è tardi, continuo.

Italian grammar reference · Section 8

Ci and ne, the two particles English cannot translate

Four letters between them, and no clean English equivalent for either — which is exactly why learners leave them out and sound foreign. Once the underlying test is clear, both become mechanical.

CINEChoosingVerbs built on themCombined formsTest yourself

CI

Four jobs

Two letters doing four different jobs. Most of the confusion comes from not noticing which job is active.

1 — A PLACE ALREADY MENTIONED
Vai in ufficio? Sì, ci vado adesso.Are you going to the office? Yes, I'm going there now.
Sei mai stato a Roma? Non ci sono mai stato.Have you ever been to Rome? I've never been there.
2 — REPLACING A + A THING OR AN IDEA
Pensi al progetto? Sì, ci penso.Are you thinking about the project? Yes, I'm thinking about it.
Credi a quello che dice? Non ci credo.Do you believe what he says? I don't believe it.
Sei riuscito a finire? Sì, ci sono riuscito.Did you manage to finish? Yes, I managed it.
3 — THERE IS, THERE ARE
C'è un problema. · Ci sono due opzioni.There's a problem. · There are two options.
Non c'era nessuno.There was nobody.
4 — EACH OTHER, WITH NOI
Ci vediamo domani.We'll see each other tomorrow.
Ci sentiamo la settimana prossima.We'll speak next week.

NE

No English equivalent

Ne replaces di plus something, or a quantity out of a larger set. It is the particle English has no equivalent for, which is why it gets dropped.

1 — QUANTITY, OUT OF A LARGER SET
Quante versioni hai? Ne ho tre.How many versions do you have? I have three (of them).
Vuoi del caffè? Sì, ne voglio un po'.Do you want some coffee? Yes, I want a bit.
Ne ho abbastanza.I've had enough.
2 — REPLACING DI + A THING OR AN IDEA
Parliamo del budget? Sì, ne parliamo domani.Shall we discuss the budget? Yes, we'll discuss it tomorrow.
Hai bisogno di aiuto? Sì, ne ho bisogno.Do you need help? Yes, I need it.
Cosa ne pensi?What do you think about it?
3 — FROM A PLACE
Sei uscito dall'ufficio? Sì, ne sono uscito ora.Did you leave the office? Yes, I left it just now.
Me ne vado.I'm leaving. — andarsene, a verb built on ne

In the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with the quantity ne refers to: Quante ne hai viste? Ne ho viste tre.

Choosing between them

The one test

The test is which preposition the verb takes. A verb that takes a gets ci. A verb that takes di gets ne.

Verbs that take A → ci

pensare a · credere a · riuscire a · abituarsi a · rinunciare a · partecipare a

Ci penso io. I'll take care of it.

Verbs that take DI → ne

parlare di · avere bisogno di · accorgersi di · dimenticarsi di · occuparsi di · innamorarsi di

Non me ne sono accorto. I didn't notice it.

Cosa ne pensi is fixed

Even though pensare normally takes a, the phrase "what do you think of it" always uses ne, because it comes from pensare di qualcosa in the sense of having an opinion.

Cosa ci pensi?Cosa ne pensi? — What do you think about it?Ci penso io. — I'll deal with it.

Do not repeat ne when the thing is named in the usual word order

If the noun appears in full after the verb, the particle is redundant. (Naming the topic first or last for emphasis is fine: Del progetto, ne parlo domani.)

Ne parlo del progetto.Parlo del progetto. · Ne parlo.

Verbs built on ci and ne

Very common

Some verbs absorb the particle and change meaning entirely. These are common in speech and rarely taught early.

volercito take, to be needed — Ci vuole tempo. / It takes time.
mettercito take (a person's time) — Ci metto un'ora. / It takes me an hour.
farcelato manage, to cope — Non ce la faccio. / I can't cope.
entrarcito be relevant — Questo non c'entra. / That's beside the point.
andarseneto leave, to go away — Me ne vado. / I'm off.
averne abbastanzato have had enough — Ne ho abbastanza.
non poterne piùto not be able to take it any more — Non ne posso più.
VOLERCI OR METTERCI
Ci vogliono due ore.It takes two hours. — in general, for anyone
Ci metto due ore.It takes me two hours. — for this specific person

Combined with other pronouns

When ci or ne meets another pronoun, the vowels shift. These forms are worth learning as whole words.

ce lo · ce la · ce li · ce leci changes to ce before another pronoun
ce n'è · ce ne sonothere is some · there are some
me ne · te ne · gliene · ce ne · ve neto me of it · to you of it · to him of it ...
IN USE
Ce n'è ancora?Is there any left?
Me ne dai due?Will you give me two of them?
Gliene ho parlato ieri.I spoke to him about it yesterday.
Non ce ne sono più.There aren't any left.

Italian grammar reference · Section 9

Words you already know without knowing it

Thousands of English words convert into Italian by changing one ending. This section is the conversion table — the fastest vocabulary gain available in the language, and the three checks that stop it backfiring.

Why it worksThe patternsWhere it stopsTest yourself

Why this works

Free vocabulary

Italian and English took a very large number of words from the same Latin source. English kept them for formal and technical registers; Italian uses them everywhere. That mismatch is in your favour: the more formal the English word, the more likely a direct Italian equivalent exists.

Prefer the Latin word, not the Germanic one

English usually has two words for one idea — one plain and Germanic, one formal and Latin. The Latin one is the one that converts.

"to begin" gives nothing, but "to commence" gives cominciare
"to buy" gives nothing, but "to acquire" gives acquistare

The ending also tells you the gender

Every pattern below comes with a fixed gender, so you get the article for free.

-zione, -sione, -tà, -anza, -enza, -ura are feminine
-mento, -ismo, -ore are masculine

The patterns

19 patterns

Nineteen endings that convert reliably. Each one is worth more vocabulary than a week of flashcards.

ENGLISH ENDING  →  ITALIAN ENDING  ·  GENDER  ·  EXAMPLES
-tion → -zione (f)information → informazione · situation → situazione · attention → attenzione
-sion → -sione (f)decision → decisione · television → televisione · pressure → pressione
-ty → -tà (f)university → università · reality → realtà · quality → qualità · city → città
-ly → -mente (adv)normally → normalmente · exactly → esattamente · rarely → raramente
-ous → -oso (adj)famous → famoso · nervous → nervoso · curious → curioso
-al → -ale (adj)normal → normale · personal → personale · digital → digitale
-ble → -bile (adj)possible → possibile · terrible → terribile · responsible → responsabile
-ic → -ico (adj)public → pubblico · specific → specifico · automatic → automatico
-ive → -ivo (adj)creative → creativo · active → attivo · negative → negativo
-ant / -ent → -ante / -ente (adj)important → importante · different → differente · elegant → elegante
-ance / -ence → -anza / -enza (f)importance → importanza · difference → differenza · patience → pazienza
-ment → -mento (m)movement → movimento · document → documento · payment → pagamento
-ist → -ista (m/f)artist → artista · journalist → giornalista · specialist → specialista
-ism → -ismo (m)tourism → turismo · realism → realismo · optimism → ottimismo
-ary → -ario (adj/m)necessary → necessario · ordinary → ordinario · salary → salario
-ure → -ura (f)structure → struttura · culture → cultura · nature → natura
-or → -ore (m)director → direttore · error → errore · color → colore
-ify → -ificare (verb)simplify → semplificare · verify → verificare · modify → modificare
-ize → -izzare (verb)organize → organizzare · realize → realizzare · analyse → analizzare

Where it stops working

Verify first

The patterns are productive, not guaranteed. Three checks before you trust one.

1 — Spelling shifts at the join

Double consonants appear where English has one, and the other way round.
attenzione (not atenzione) · professione · comunicazione (one m)

2 — The stress moves

Italian almost always stresses the second-to-last syllable. uni-ver-si-tà is the exception that proves it — words in -tà stress the final syllable.

3 — Sometimes the word exists but means something else

This is common enough to have its own section. Check section 8 before using a word that looks too easy.

4 — Some common words simply do not convert

"job" is not giobbo, it is lavoro. "nice" is not nico, it is simpatico or bello.

Italian grammar reference · Section 10

Words that look familiar and are not

The previous section showed how much English vocabulary converts straight into Italian. This one is the correction: the words where that instinct produces a sentence that is fluent, confident and wrong.

The listWorst offendersTest yourself

Thirty words that are not what they look like

Search enabled

Search by either language. The third column gives the word you probably wanted and how to say it correctly.

ITALIAN WORD  ·  WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEANS  ·  THE ENGLISH WORD YOU MEANT, AND ITS REAL TRANSLATION
attualmentecurrently, at present“actually” is in realtà, veramente
eventualmentepossibly, if need be“eventually” is alla fine, prima o poi
parentirelatives“parents” is i genitori
libreriabookshop“library” is la biblioteca
fattoriafarm“factory” is la fabbrica
cameraroom, bedroom“camera” is la macchina fotografica
morbidosoft“morbid” is morboso
sensibilesensitive“sensible” is ragionevole
educatopolite, well-mannered“educated” is istruito, colto
pretendereto demand, to claim“to pretend” is fingere
argomentotopic, subject“argument (quarrel)” is litigio, discussione
annoiareto bore“to annoy” is infastidire, dare fastidio
assistereto attend, to witness“to assist” is aiutare
domandareto ask“to demand” is esigere, pretendere
firmasignature“firm, company” is l'azienda, la ditta
magazzinowarehouse, storeroom“magazine” is la rivista
noiosoboring“noisy” is rumoroso
rumorenoise“rumour” is la voce, la diceria
simpaticolikeable, nice“sympathetic” is comprensivo
confidenzafamiliarity, closeness“confidence (self-belief)” is fiducia in sé
fabbricafactory“fabric” is il tessuto, la stoffa
cantinacellar“canteen” is la mensa
preservativocondom“preservative” is il conservante
lussurialust“luxury” is il lusso
crudoraw, uncooked“crude” is rozzo, grezzo
stanzaroom“stanza (of a poem)” is la strofa
ultimamenterecently, lately“ultimately” is in definitiva, alla fine
occorrereto be necessary“to occur” is accadere, succedere
realizzareto carry out, to achieve“to realise (understand)” is rendersi conto, capire
addizioneaddition (arithmetic)“addition (extra thing)” is aggiunta
Nothing matches that.

The four worst offenders

Read twice

These four appear constantly in professional writing, and getting them wrong changes the meaning of the sentence rather than just sounding odd.

attualmente does not mean actually

It means currently. Using it for "actually" reverses your meaning in a way the reader will not catch.

Attualmente non è quello che intendevo. (reads: currently it isn't what I meant)In realtà non è quello che intendevo. — actually, that isn't what I meantAttualmente lavoro a Milano. — I currently work in Milan

eventualmente does not mean eventually

It means possibly, or if necessary. In an email this can commit you to something you did not intend.

Eventualmente ti mando il file. (reads: I'll send it if need be)Prima o poi ti mando il file. — I'll send it eventuallyEventualmente possiamo rimandare. — if necessary, we can postpone

pretendere does not mean to pretend

It means to demand. In a work context this makes you sound far more aggressive than intended.

Pretendo di capire. (reads: I demand to understand)Fingo di capire. — I pretend to understandPretende un aumento. — he is demanding a raise

educato does not mean educated

It means well-mannered. Saying someone is not educato is a comment on their manners, not their schooling.

È una persona molto educata. (reads: very polite, not highly educated)È una persona molto istruita. — a highly educated personÈ molto educato. — he is very polite

Italian grammar reference · Section 11

Tu, Lei, and writing an email that lands

Italian draws the line between formal and informal more sharply than English, and formal correspondence follows conventions closely enough that following them correctly reads as competence. This section is the pattern, in both directions.

Tu & LeiFormal emailInformalFixed phrasesTest yourself

Tu and Lei

The core mechanic

Italian has two ways of saying "you", and the formal one is not a separate set of endings — it is the third person singular, as if addressing the person indirectly.

How Lei works

Lei takes the same verb form as lui or lei.

Come sta? How are you? — formal
Come stai? How are you? — informal

Object pronouns follow: La for direct, Le for indirect.
La ringrazio. · Le scrivo domani.

Capitalised in writing

In formal writing, the pronouns referring to the reader take a capital: Lei, La, Le, Suo, Sua. This is a courtesy convention, and its absence is noticed in professional email.

La ringrazio per la Sua disponibilità.
WHICH ONE TO USE
Leistrangers, officials, professors, clients, anyone older you don't know, all first written contact
tufriends, family, colleagues at the same level, children, and anyone who has offered it
voiany group, formal or not — Italian has no formal plural in everyday use
SWITCHING
Possiamo darci del tu?Shall we use tu with each other? — the standard way to propose it
Dammi pure del tu.Please use tu with me. — the standard way to offer it

Default to Lei with anyone in an academic or professional setting until they switch first. Being unnecessarily formal reads as polite; being unnecessarily informal reads as careless.

The structure of a formal email

Copy the pattern

Italian formal correspondence is more conventional than English. Following the pattern signals competence more than fluent vocabulary does.

1 — OPENING
Gentile Dottor Rossi, · Gentile Dottoressa Rossi,Dear Dr Rossi — the standard, for anyone with a degree
Gentile Professor Rossi, · Gentile Professoressa Rossi,for academics
Egregio Signor Rossi,more formal still, slightly old-fashioned
Spettabile Segreteria, · Alla cortese attenzione di...to an office rather than a person
Buongiorno,acceptable when you do not know the name
2 — WHY YOU ARE WRITING
Le scrivo in merito a...I am writing regarding...
La contatto per chiedere informazioni su...I am contacting you to ask for information about...
Faccio seguito alla Sua email del 12 marzo.Further to your email of 12 March.
3 — THE REQUEST
Le sarei grato se potesse...I would be grateful if you could... — note the subjunctive
Vorrei sapere se è possibile...I would like to know whether it is possible...
Le chiedo cortesemente di...I kindly ask you to...
In allegato trova la documentazione richiesta.Attached you will find the requested documentation.
4 — CLOSING
Resto a disposizione per ulteriori chiarimenti.I remain available for any further clarification.
In attesa di un Suo riscontro,Awaiting your reply,
La ringrazio anticipatamente.Thank you in advance.
5 — SIGN-OFF
Cordiali saluti,Kind regards — the safe default
Distinti saluti,Yours sincerely — more formal
Cordialmente,Regards — slightly lighter

Informal writing

Ciao Marco, · Caro Marco, · Cara Giulia,Hi Marco · Dear Marco · Dear Giulia
Come va? · Tutto bene?How's it going? · All good?
Ti scrivo solo per dirti che...I'm just writing to tell you that...
Fammi sapere.Let me know.
A presto! · Ci sentiamo!See you soon! · Talk soon!
Un abbraccio · Un caro salutoA hug · Warm wishes — normal between friends, not at work

Phrases that carry the register

Fixed forms

The vocabulary is not more difficult — it is more conventional. These are the fixed forms an Italian reader expects.

Formal

Resto a disposizione. I remain available.
La ringrazio per l'attenzione. Thank you for your attention.
Come da accordi, As agreed,
Con riferimento a... With reference to...
Le porgo i miei più cordiali saluti. My warmest regards.

Neutral and safe anywhere

Grazie mille. Thanks very much.
Ti/Le allego il file. I'm attaching the file.
Fammi/Mi faccia sapere. Let me know.
Scusa/Scusi il ritardo. Sorry for the delay.

Do not translate "Dear" as Caro in a formal email

Caro is affectionate. To a professor, a client or an office it reads as over-familiar.

Caro Professor Rossi,Gentile Professor Rossi,

Do not sign off a work email with Baci or Un bacio

These are for close friends and family only. The mistake is memorable in the wrong way.

Baci, MarcoCordiali saluti, Marco

Italian grammar reference · Section 12

The errors that outlive everything else

These are not beginner mistakes. They are the ones that persist into B1 and B2, because each one is grammatical enough to pass unnoticed while you are writing. Every entry gives the rule, not just the correction.

The logHow to use it

Twenty errors that survive longest

Search enabled

Each entry gives the wrong form, the correct one, and the rule underneath — because a correction you cannot derive is a correction you will need again.

Dropping the reflexive pronounSveglio alle sette.Mi sveglio alle sette.Reflexive verbs carry a pronoun in every person. Without it the verb means you wake someone else up.
A past tense for an ongoing actionHo lavorato qui da tre anni.Lavoro qui da tre anni.DA plus the PRESENT for anything that started in the past and is still true.
prima che where prima di belongsPrima che io esca, controllo tutto.Prima di uscire, controllo tutto.Same subject takes prima di plus the infinitive. Different subjects take prima che plus the subjunctive.
Half a negativeHo visto niente. · Sono stato mai in Italia.Non ho visto niente. · Non sono mai stato in Italia.Italian negation needs both halves: non before the verb, and the negative word after it.
Adding a preposition English needsAspetto per il treno. · Ascolto alla musica.Aspetto il treno. · Ascolto la musica.aspettare, ascoltare, guardare, cercare and pagare take a direct object with no preposition.
The wrong auxiliaryHo andato al lavoro.Sono andato al lavoro.Verbs of motion and change of state take essere, and the participle agrees with the subject.
No agreement after essereLei è andato. · Siamo arrivato.Lei è andata. · Siamo arrivati.With essere the participle agrees in gender and number. With avere it does not.
An article where none belongsSono un ingegnere. · Mio il padre.Sono ingegnere. · Mio padre.No article after essere with a profession, and none before a single family member.
An indicative after a subjunctive triggerPenso che è giusto. · Benché è tardi.Penso che sia giusto. · Benché sia tardi.Opinion, doubt, emotion and will take the congiuntivo — and so do benché, sebbene, purché and prima che.
anche se treated like benchéAnche se sia tardi.Anche se è tardi.anche se is the one concessive that keeps the indicative.
Leaving out ci or nePenso al progetto. Sì, penso.Ci penso. · Ne parlo domani.Verbs taking a get ci; verbs taking di get ne. Omitting them is grammatical but audibly foreign.
Dropping the relative pronounIl file ho mandato.Il file che ho mandato.English can omit "that". Italian never can.
qualche with a plural nounqualche giorniqualche giorno · alcuni giorniqualche always takes a singular noun even though it means "a few".
Gender agreement drifti vestiti nuove · una problemai vestiti nuovi · un problemaAdjectives follow their noun. Nouns in -ma from Greek are usually masculine: problema, sistema, tema.
No capital after a full stop...finito. poi sono uscito....finito. Poi sono uscito.Basic, but it is what a reader notices first in written work.
qual è written with an apostrophequal'èqual èqual is a truncated form, not an elided one, so it takes no apostrophe.
Confusing buono and beneParlo buono l'italiano. · Il caffè è bene.Parlo bene l'italiano. · Il caffè è buono.buono describes a thing, bene describes an action.
Translating attualmente as actuallyAttualmente non intendevo questo.In realtà non intendevo questo.attualmente means currently. See section 8.
Cardinal number where an ordinal belongsil uno maggioil primo maggioOnly the first of the month uses an ordinal. Every other day uses a cardinal.
Missing contractionil nome di il cliente · vado a il lavoroil nome del cliente · vado al lavorodi, a, da, in and su must fuse with a following definite article.
Nothing matches that.

How to use this page

Diagnose, do not memorise

Every entry names a rule. If you can state the rule, you will catch the error in a sentence you have never seen. If you only remember the example, you will only catch that example.

Track your own

The list is deliberately general. Keep your own additions beside it — the errors you personally repeat are worth more attention than the ones you have never made.

Check writing against this page before sending

Most of these survive because they are invisible while writing and obvious while reading. A single pass against this list catches the majority.

The three highest-value rules

If you fix only three things: DA plus the present, the auxiliary and its agreement, and the subjunctive after opinion. Together they account for most of what marks a B1 writer as a B1 writer.

A2Vorrei un biglietto di andata e ritorno.I'd like a return ticket.
A2Dove posso lasciare i bagagli?Where can I leave my luggage?
A2Scendo alla prossima fermata.I'm getting off at the next stop.
B1Ho prenotato un volo per martedì, ma vorrei cambiare la data.I booked a flight for Tuesday, but I'd like to change the date.
B1Il treno è stato cancellato, quindi dobbiamo trovare un'alternativa.The train has been cancelled, so we have to find an alternative.
B1Se perdo la coincidenza, arriverò con due ore di ritardo.If I miss the connection, I'll arrive two hours late.
B1Quando siamo arrivati in aeroporto, il volo era già partito.When we got to the airport, the flight had already left.trapassato prossimo
B1La compagnia ha perso la mia valigia e non so a chi rivolgermi.The airline has lost my suitcase and I don't know who to ask.
B1Preferisco viaggiare in treno perché posso lavorare durante il viaggio.I prefer travelling by train because I can work during the journey.
B2Se fossi partito mezz'ora prima, non avrei perso il volo.If I had left half an hour earlier, I wouldn't have missed the flight.periodo ipotetico (3rd type)
B2Abbiamo visitato la città senza fretta, lasciandoci guidare dalla curiosità.We explored the city unhurriedly, letting curiosity guide us.gerundio
B2Benché il viaggio sia stato lungo, ne è valsa la pena.Although the journey was long, it was worth it.
B2Pensavo di arrivare in orario, ma il treno ha avuto un guasto.I thought I'd arrive on time, but the train broke down.
B2Vorrei sapere se è previsto un rimborso per il ritardo.I'd like to know whether a refund is provided for the delay.
AdvViaggiare non significa solo vedere posti nuovi, ma imparare a uscire dalla propria zona di comfort.Travelling doesn't just mean seeing new places, but learning to step outside your comfort zone.
AdvPer quanto mi riguarda, i viaggi migliori sono quelli che non si programmano troppo.As far as I'm concerned, the best trips are the ones you don't over-plan.
AdvCi siamo persi, ma è proprio così che abbiamo scoperto il posto più bello del viaggio.We got lost, but that's exactly how we discovered the best place of the trip.

Health & body

A1Non sto bene.I'm not well.
A1Ho mal di testa.I have a headache.
A1Ho mal di gola.I have a sore throat.
A1Ho la febbre.I have a fever.
A1Ho bisogno di un medico.I need a doctor.
A1Mi fa male la schiena.My back hurts.
A2Ho la tosse e il raffreddore da due giorni.I've had a cough and a cold for two days.
A2Dov'è la farmacia più vicina?Where's the nearest pharmacy?
A2Quante volte al giorno devo prendere questa medicina?How many times a day should I take this medicine?
A2Ieri avevo la febbre, ma oggi sto meglio.Yesterday I had a fever, but today I feel better.
A2Vorrei prendere un appuntamento dal dottore.I'd like to make an appointment with the doctor.
A2Mi sono fatto male al ginocchio.I hurt my knee.
A2Devo restare a letto?Do I have to stay in bed?
B1Da quando ho cambiato lavoro dormo male e mi sento sempre stanco.Since I changed jobs I've been sleeping badly and I always feel tired.
B1Il medico mi ha consigliato di riposare e di bere molta acqua.The doctor advised me to rest and drink plenty of water.
B1Se la febbre non passa entro domani, vado al pronto soccorso.If the fever doesn't go down by tomorrow, I'll go to A&E.
B1Il medico mi ha fatto una ricetta per degli antibiotici.The doctor gave me a prescription for antibiotics.
B1Dovrei fare più movimento, ma non ho mai tempo.I should get more exercise, but I never have time.condizionale
B2Non credo che sia niente di grave, ma preferisco farmi controllare.I don't think it's anything serious, but I'd rather get checked.congiuntivo
B2Se avessi dormito di più, adesso non mi sentirei così a pezzi.If I'd slept more, I wouldn't feel so worn out now.mixed conditional
B2Il dottore vuole che faccia degli esami del sangue prima della visita.The doctor wants me to have blood tests before the appointment.volere che + congiuntivo
B2Ho un dolore che va e viene, soprattutto quando mi piego.I have a pain that comes and goes, especially when I bend over.
B2Ho iniziato a camminare ogni giorno e mi sento molto meglio.I've started walking every day and I feel much better.
AdvPiù che di una cura, ho bisogno di un po' di riposo.More than a treatment, I need a bit of rest.
AdvSebbene i sintomi siano lievi, è bene non sottovalutarli.Although the symptoms are mild, it's best not to underestimate them.
AdvMi sono sempre fidato più del mio corpo che delle diagnosi trovate su internet.I've always trusted my body more than diagnoses found on the internet.

Free time & weather

A1Che tempo fa oggi?What's the weather like today?
A1Oggi piove.It's raining today.
A1Fa caldo. · Fa freddo.It's hot. · It's cold.
A1Nel tempo libero leggo e ascolto musica.In my free time I read and listen to music.
A1Mi piace camminare.I like walking.
A1Domani c'è il sole.Tomorrow it's sunny.
A2Ti va di prendere un caffè?Do you fancy a coffee?informal
A2Sabato andiamo al cinema, vuoi venire?We're going to the cinema on Saturday, do you want to come?
A2Che programmi hai per il fine settimana?What plans do you have for the weekend?
A2Domani nevicherà in montagna.It'll snow in the mountains tomorrow.futuro semplice
A2Il fine settimana scorso sono andato al mare.Last weekend I went to the seaside.
A2Mi piacciono molto le mostre d'arte.I really like art exhibitions.
A2Ho comprato due biglietti per il concerto.I bought two tickets for the concert.
B1Se domani fa bel tempo, facciamo un picnic al parco.If the weather's nice tomorrow, let's have a picnic in the park.se + presente
B1Da bambino giocavo a calcio ogni pomeriggio.As a child I played football every afternoon.imperfetto
B1Non vedo l'ora di partire per le vacanze.I can't wait to go on holiday.
B1Stavo per uscire quando ha cominciato a piovere.I was about to go out when it started raining.stare per + infinito
B1Sono andato a vedere una mostra bellissima: te la consiglio.I went to see a wonderful exhibition: I recommend it.
B1Ho bisogno di staccare un po' dal lavoro.I need to switch off from work for a bit.
B2Non vedo l'ora che arrivino le vacanze.I can't wait for the holidays to arrive.non vedo l'ora che + congiuntivo
B2Se non fosse piovuto, saremmo andati in bicicletta.If it hadn't rained, we'd have gone cycling.periodo ipotetico (3rd type)
B2Mi piacerebbe imparare a suonare uno strumento, ma temo che sia troppo tardi.I'd love to learn an instrument, but I'm afraid it's too late.
B2Abbiamo deciso di rimandare la gita, a meno che il tempo non migliori.We've decided to postpone the trip, unless the weather improves.
B2Il film, pur essendo lungo, non annoia mai.The film, though long, is never boring.
AdvQuando il tempo lo permette, preferisco passare i weekend all'aria aperta.When the weather allows it, I prefer to spend weekends outdoors.
AdvNon c'è niente come un pomeriggio senza impegni per rimettere in ordine i pensieri.There's nothing like an afternoon with no commitments for putting your thoughts back in order.
AdvPiù che il posto in sé, a farmi stare bene è il fatto di non avere fretta.More than the place itself, what makes me feel good is not being in a hurry.

Work & study

A1Lavoro in un ufficio.I work in an office.
A1Sono uno studente.I'm a student.
A1Studio all'università.I study at the university.
A1Che lavoro fai?What do you do for a living?informal
A1Domani non lavoro.I'm not working tomorrow.
A2Lavoro in una piccola azienda da cinque anni.I've worked at a small company for five years.da + presente
A2Ho una riunione alle tre.I have a meeting at three.
A2Oggi finisco presto.I'm finishing early today.
A2Devo mandare un'email al cliente.I have to send an email to the client.
A2Frequento un corso di italiano due volte a settimana.I attend an Italian course twice a week.
A2Domani ho un esame importante.I have an important exam tomorrow.
A2Ti mando il file entro stasera.I'll send you the file by this evening.entro = by (a deadline)
B1Possiamo fissare una riunione per giovedì?Can we set a meeting for Thursday?
B1Ho bisogno di un paio di giorni in più.I need a couple more days.
B1Il progetto è in ritardo di una settimana.The project is a week behind.
B1Chi si occupa di questa parte?Who is handling this part?
B1Confermo la mia presenza.I confirm I'll be there.
B1Lavoro come ingegnere da più di dieci anni.I've worked as an engineer for more than ten years.da + presente
B1Il mio obiettivo più importante è raggiungere il livello B2 entro l'anno prossimo.My most important goal is to reach B2 level by next year.più + aggettivo, entro
B1Ho intenzione di iscrivermi a una laurea magistrale in Italia.I intend to enrol in a master's degree in Italy.iscriversi a (not "studiare la laurea")
B1L'anno prossimo studierò in Italia.Next year I'll study in Italy.futuro: studierò, not studiarò
B1Ho un colloquio di lavoro domani e sono un po' nervoso.I have a job interview tomorrow and I'm a bit nervous.
B1Prima lavoravo come dipendente, ora sono libero professionista.I used to be an employee, now I'm self-employed.

B2Faccio il punto e ti aggiorno.I'll take stock and update you.
B2Vorrei proporre un'alternativa.I'd like to propose an alternative.
B2Sono disposto a lavorare di più, purché le condizioni siano chiare.I'm willing to work more, provided the terms are clear.purché + congiuntivo
B2Il cliente ha chiesto delle modifiche che non erano previste nel preventivo.The client asked for changes that weren't included in the quote.
B2Se me l'avessi detto prima, avrei potuto organizzarmi meglio.If you'd told me sooner, I could have organised myself better.periodo ipotetico (3rd type)
B2Mi è stato chiesto di presentare il progetto davanti a tutto il team.I've been asked to present the project in front of the whole team.passivo
B2Il progetto dovrebbe essere consegnato entro la fine del mese.The project should be delivered by the end of the month.
B2Il budget è limitato, quindi dobbiamo stabilire le priorità.The budget is limited, so we have to set priorities.
B2Il corso si tiene interamente in italiano, per questo studio la lingua ogni giorno.The course is held entirely in Italian, which is why I study the language every day.
AdvA mio avviso, il problema non è la mancanza di tempo, ma la mancanza di priorità.In my view, the problem isn't lack of time but lack of priorities.
AdvAvrei preferito che mi avessero avvisato prima di cambiare la scadenza.I'd have preferred them to warn me before changing the deadline.condizionale passato + congiuntivo trapassato
AdvMi preme sottolineare che i tempi di consegna dipendono anche dal vostro riscontro.I'd like to stress that delivery times also depend on your feedback.formal
AdvUn buon progetto nasce da un buon brief, non dai ritocchi dell'ultimo minuto.A good project comes from a good brief, not from last-minute tweaks.
AdvNon è questione di capacità, ma di organizzazione: se ci fossimo mossi prima, ora non saremmo sotto pressione.It isn't a question of ability but of organisation: if we'd started earlier, we wouldn't be under pressure now.mixed conditional

B2Ai sensi del regolamento, la richiesta va presentata entro trenta giorni.Under the regulations, the request must be submitted within thirty days.formal

AdvCol senno di poi, avrei agito diversamente.With hindsight, I'd have acted differently.

Levels are a guide: they reflect the grammar and vocabulary a sentence needs, in line with typical coursebook progression, not an official CEFR classification.

How to drill these

Cover the Italian, not the English

Reading Italian and recognising the meaning is passive. Reading the English and producing the Italian is the skill you actually need. Switch on “Hide Italian” above, say the sentence aloud, then tap the row to check yourself.

Say them aloud

These are spoken sentences. Reading them silently trains the wrong channel — the goal is for them to arrive without assembly, which only happens through the mouth.

Change one element at a time

Take Ti mando il file entro stasera and swap the object, then the time, then the person. One sentence becomes twenty patterns.

Add your own as you meet them

The best sentences in any bank are the ones you needed and did not have. Keep adding — a bank that stops growing stops being useful.

Test yourself

Self-marking

Ten questions drawn from a larger bank, different each time. You see the correction and the rule after every answer, and anything you miss goes into your mistake log.

Italian grammar reference · Section 14

Where to get the input you need

Grammar reference gets you to correct. Volume of real Italian gets you to fluent. Everything listed here is free or has a substantial free tier, and every link goes to the source rather than an aggregator.

ListeningReadingVideoToolsCertificationsWeekly plan

Listening

Start here

Listening is the slowest skill to build and the one exams weight most heavily. Daily contact matters more than length of session.

Coffee Break Italian A1–B1

https://coffeebreaklanguages.com/coffeebreakitalian/

Structured audio course from absolute beginner upwards. Free episodes on all podcast apps; the paid tier adds materials. Best used on commutes.

Podcast Italiano B1–C1

https://podcastitaliano.com

Slow and normal-speed episodes on culture, language and current topics, with free transcripts. The bridge between graded material and real Italian.

Easy Italian B1–B2

https://www.easyitalian.fm

Street interviews and conversational episodes with transcripts. Unscripted speech at natural speed, which is what exams test.

RAI Play Radio B2+

https://www.raiplaysound.it

The national broadcaster's full radio archive, free. News, documentaries and drama — unfiltered native speed.

Reading and dictionaries

Il Post B1–B2

https://www.ilpost.it

Clear, well-edited Italian news. Shorter sentences than the traditional papers, which makes it the best first newspaper.

Internazionale B2+

https://www.internazionale.it

World journalism translated into Italian. Familiar subject matter carries you through unfamiliar vocabulary.

Treccani B1+

https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/

The authoritative Italian dictionary, free online. Use it once definitions in Italian stop being intimidating — monolingual lookup accelerates everything.

WordReference All

https://www.wordreference.com/iten/

Bilingual dictionary with the best forum discussions on usage anywhere. Search a phrase, not just a word.

Video

Learn Italian with Lucrezia A2–B2

https://www.youtube.com/@LearnItalianwithLucrezia

Grammar explained in Italian at a controlled pace, plus vlogs. The clearest free explanations of the subjunctive available.

LearnAmo A1–C1

https://learnamo.com

Video lessons and written articles covering grammar, idioms and exam preparation. Strong on the errors foreigners actually make.

RAI Play B1+

https://www.raiplay.it

Free Italian television with Italian subtitles on much of the catalogue. Documentaries are easier than drama — start there.

Tools

Anki All

https://apps.ankiweb.net

Spaced-repetition flashcards, free on desktop and Android. The only vocabulary tool that reliably survives a year of use.

Reverso Context All

https://context.reverso.net/translation/italian-english/

Shows a word inside thousands of real bilingual sentences. Use it to check whether a phrase is actually said, not just grammatical.

The three official certifications

B2 for university

All three are recognised by the Italian state. For university admission the level required is B2 — CILS Due or CELI 3. Choose by which centre is reachable from where you live, not by reputation; they are equivalent.

CILS — Università per Stranieri di Siena Official

https://www.unistrasi.it

Sat twice a year, in early June and December, on the same day at every centre worldwide. CILS Due B2 is the level that opens Italian university admission.

CELI — Università per Stranieri di Perugia Official

https://www.cvcl.unistrapg.it

Multiple sessions per year. CELI 3 is the B2 level recognised for university enrolment. Run through the CVCL centre.

PLIDA — Società Dante Alighieri Official

https://plida.it

Issued by the Dante Alighieri Society and recognised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Frequent sessions, and the widest network of centres abroad.

Building a week from these

Daily, non-negotiable

Twenty minutes of listening and ten minutes of flashcards. Both work on commutes, which is why they survive busy weeks.

Three times a week

One article read properly — looked-up words added to flashcards the same day. Reading without capturing vocabulary is entertainment, not study.

Once a week

One piece of writing, one conversation. These are the productive skills, and they only improve through production. Everything else is input.

Before the exam

Six months out, switch listening to unsubtitled native speed and start timed writing. The exam tests speed under pressure, which is a separate skill from knowing the grammar.

The two B2 exams compared

Check the current call

The two certificates most universities and conservatoires accept at B2. Which one an institution accepts, and at what level, is set by each institution's own call for applications, so read that before you book.

CELI 3 (B2)CILS B2
Issued byUniversità per Stranieri di PerugiaUniversità per Stranieri di Siena
PartsA reading · B writing · C language competence · D listening · oral examListening · reading · analysis of communication structures · written production · oral production
WeightReading 20% · writing 20% · language competence 10% · listening 20% · oral 30%Five parts, each worth up to 20 points
Scoring200 points in total: 140 written (A–D) and 60 oral100 points in total
To passAt least 84 on the written papers and 33 on the oral, and 117 or more overall (grades A, B or C)At least 11 points in each part, and 55 or more overall
What it rewardsBalanced skills: the oral alone is 30% of the markEvery skill counts equally: one weak part can sink the result

Thresholds are taken from the universities' published scoring documents (CELI 3 scoring and the CILS evaluation procedures). Durations, dates and fees change by session, so confirm them with the official site or your exam centre.

How this reference trains for them

• The B2 level exam on the Tests page checks the grammar both exams assume.
• The writing templates below match the two kinds of text you are asked for: a formal letter and an opinion text.
• The speaking trainer rehearses the monologue and the discussion in the oral part.

Where candidates lose points

• Skipping the oral practice until the last month.
• Writing short, safe sentences instead of using connectors and the congiuntivo.
• Ignoring the listening part: it needs regular real Italian, not just grammar.
• Misjudging time in the written papers.

Writing templates

Copy the structure

Replace everything in [brackets] with your own details. The phrases beneath each model are the ones that carry the register: reuse them.

Formal email to a university office B1–B2

Oggetto: Richiesta di informazioni sull'iscrizione al corso di laurea magistrale in [corso]

Gentile Segreteria,

mi chiamo [nome e cognome] e Le scrivo per chiedere alcune informazioni sull'iscrizione al corso di laurea magistrale in [corso] per l'anno accademico [anno].

Più precisamente, vorrei sapere:
1) quali documenti devo presentare;
2) entro quale data va inviata la domanda;
3) se è richiesta una certificazione linguistica e di quale livello.

In allegato trova il mio curriculum.

La ringrazio per l'attenzione e resto a disposizione per qualsiasi chiarimento.

Cordiali saluti,
[nome e cognome]
Phrases to reuse
Le scrivo per chiedere…Più precisamente, vorrei sapere…In allegato trova…Resto a disposizione per…La ringrazio anticipatamente.

Formal complaint B2

Oggetto: Segnalazione di un problema relativo all'ordine n. [numero]

Gentile Servizio Clienti,

Le scrivo per segnalare un problema con l'ordine n. [numero], effettuato il [data].

Il prodotto è arrivato con tre giorni di ritardo e presenta un difetto: [descrizione]. Purtroppo, nonostante abbia già contattato il vostro servizio telefonico, nessuno ha risolto la situazione.

Vi chiedo pertanto di sostituire il prodotto oppure di rimborsare l'importo versato. Sarei grato se poteste darmi un riscontro entro sette giorni.

In attesa di una Vostra risposta, porgo cordiali saluti.
[nome e cognome]
Phrases to reuse
Le scrivo per segnalare…Purtroppo…Vi chiedo pertanto di…Sarei grato se poteste…In attesa di una Vostra risposta,

Opinion essay (B2 model) B2

Negli ultimi anni il lavoro da remoto è diventato una realtà per milioni di persone, e molti si chiedono se migliori davvero la qualità della vita. A mio avviso la risposta dipende dal modo in cui questo strumento viene usato.

Da un lato, lavorare da casa fa risparmiare tempo e denaro, perché si evitano gli spostamenti, e permette di organizzare meglio la giornata. Inoltre, chi ha una famiglia riesce spesso a conciliare più facilmente gli impegni.

Dall'altro lato, non bisogna sottovalutare i rischi: senza confini chiari tra lavoro e vita privata, si finisce per lavorare di più, e la mancanza di contatto con i colleghi può portare all'isolamento.

In conclusione, ritengo che lo smart working sia un vantaggio, purché sia regolato da regole precise e affiancato da momenti di incontro in presenza.
Phrases to reuse
Introduzione: presenta il tema e la tua posizione (a mio avviso, secondo me)Argomento 1: da un lato… inoltre…Argomento 2 / obiezione: dall'altro lato… tuttavia…Conclusione: in conclusione, ritengo che… purché…

Informal message to a friend A2–B1

Ciao Marco,

come stai? Io sto bene, ma sono molto impegnato con il lavoro. Ti scrivo perché sabato sera faccio una cena a casa mia e mi farebbe piacere se venissi anche tu. Cominciamo verso le otto. Se vuoi, porta un dolce!

Fammi sapere se riesci a venire.

Un abbraccio,
[nome]
Phrases to reuse
Ti scrivo perché…Mi farebbe piacere se venissi…Fammi sapere…Un abbraccio, / A presto!

Gentile Commissione,

In [numero] anni di esperienza come [professione] ho sviluppato competenze in [ambito], ma ho sentito il bisogno di approfondire [tema] con una formazione strutturata. Il vostro corso, in particolare [aspetto del corso], mi sembra il percorso ideale per raggiungere questo obiettivo.

Sono convinto che il confronto con docenti e studenti di altri Paesi mi permetterà di crescere sia dal punto di vista professionale sia da quello personale. Sono inoltre consapevole che studiare in Italia significherà affrontare nuove sfide, a cominciare dalla lingua, che sto studiando da [periodo] con costanza.

Pronunciation essentials

Tap to hear

Italian is spelled almost as it is spoken, so a few rules cover nearly everything. If your device has an Italian voice, switch on Audio in the top bar and tap any Italian word below to hear it.

SpellingSoundExamples
c + e / i= "ch" as in churchcena, cinema, ciao
ch + e / i= hard "k"che, chilo, anche
g + e / i= "j" as in gingente, giorno, giovane
gh + e / i= hard "g"spaghetti, ghiaccio
sc + e / i= "sh"pesce, scena, sciare
sch + e / i= "sk"schema, schiena
gn= "ny" as in canyongnocchi, lavagna, ogni
gli= "ly" as in millionfiglio, famiglia, gli
zsounds like "ts" or "dz"grazie (ts), zero (dz)
hsilentho, hai, ha, hanno

Double consonants are long

Hold the consonant for twice as long. It changes the word:
pala ≠ pallacaro ≠ carrosete ≠ settenono ≠ nonnopena ≠ pennacasa ≠ cassacapello ≠ cappellocopia ≠ coppia

Stress

Most words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: ca-ni-ne. A written accent appears only when the stress falls on the last vowel: città, università, perché, caffè. Many verbs differ by stress alone: parlo (I speak) and parlò (he spoke); capitano (captain) and càpitano (they happen).
Vowels are pure and never reduced: a as in father, e as in bed or they, i as in machine, o as in more, u as in rule. Every vowel is pronounced, including the last one.
